entry.title: Re: #COE#CCS Can SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud support SSO wit...
entry.content:
Hi,

S/4HANA Public Cloud (S4HC) never trusts an external IdP directly. IAS acts as a proxy IdP — it sits between S4HC and your ADFS, brokering authentication. You cannot configure ADFS directly in S4HC's trust settings. For more info: 

https://help.sap.com/docs/SAP_S4HANA_CLOUD/53e36b5493804bcdb3f6f14de8b487dd/35b0aae87c5442bb9e2618ce033760bb.html

Recommended Architecture Options for DC location concern:

Option A — Best: Deploy ADFS node inside Mainland China

  • Deploy an ADFS Farm (or a WAP proxy node) inside mainland China, connected to your corporate AD via a dedicated WAN/leased line.
  • All IAS ↔ ADFS SAML traffic stays within China — lowest latency, most reliable.
  • This is the recommended approach for production systems.

Option B — Acceptable: ADFS in Hong Kong with optimised connectivity

  • If a China deployment of ADFS is not feasible, Hong Kong is the next-best option.
  • Cross-border RTT between mainland China and HK is typically 20–60ms, acceptable for interactive SAML flows.
  • Requires that your corporate network permits cross-border SAML redirects without proxying/blocking.

Option C — Avoid: ADFS only in Europe or Americas

  • Cross-border latency (200–400ms+) combined with multiple browser SAML redirects will result in noticeably slow logins (5–10+ seconds P95), and is a congestion/reliability risk.
  • Microsoft ADFS SQL Latency guidance confirms that cross-DC dependencies significantly affect ADFS throughput.

 

The flow is a 3-way metadata exchange between ADFS, IAS, and S4HC.

Step 1 — Get the ADFS Metadata

On your ADFS server, download the federation metadata XML from:

https://<your-adfs-server>/FederationMetadata/2007-06/FederationMetadata.xml

Step 2 — Register ADFS in IAS

  1. Log into the IAS Admin Console → Identity Providers → Corporate Identity Providers
  2. Click Add → upload the ADFS metadata XML
  3. Set Identity Provider Type = Microsoft ADFS / Entra ID
  4. Save, then download the IAS metadata XML (Tenant Settings → SAML 2.0 Configuration)

Step 3 — Register IAS in ADFS

  1. In AD FS Management → Relying Party Trusts → Add Relying Party Trust
  2. Import the IAS metadata XML downloaded in Step 2
  3. Add a Claim Issuance Rule: send the user's Email Address as Name ID (Email format)

Step 4 — Point S4HC Application to ADFS

  1. In IAS Admin Console → Applications → find your S/4HANA Cloud app
  2. Under Conditional Authentication, set the default IdP to the ADFS Corporate IdP created in Step 2

Step 5 — Align User Identities

Ensure the email / login name in Active Directory matches the user record in both IAS and S4HC. This is what ties the SAML assertion to the correct SAP user.

entry.title: RE-FX Considerations During Subsequent Implementation of a Further Accounting Principle (SIL)
entry.content:
Hello SAP Community,

We are preparing a Subsequent Implementation of a Further Accounting Principle (SIL) in an existing production SAP S/4HANA environment to introduce a new US GAAP parallel ledger.

Only a subset of US company codes is included in the SIL project, and some of these company codes actively use Flexible Real Estate Management (RE-FX).

According to SAP documentation, “the subsequent implementation of a further accounting principle isn't supported for Flexible Real Estate Management (RE-FX).” Based on our discussions with SAP Support, we also understand that RE-FX postings should be avoided during the implementation year until SIL is completed to prevent potential inconsistencies during data transfer.

Our main question is how this restriction should be interpreted in practice. Does RE-FX activity need to be stopped from the beginning of the fiscal year until SIL completion, or only during the actual SIL execution window?

We would also like to understand what exactly is affected by this limitation. Are FI postings generated from RE-FX correctly transferred to the new ledger, or are there specific restrictions related to contracts, cash flows, valuations, or periodic postings?

For productive systems where stopping RE-FX activity for an extended period is not feasible, what mitigation approach is recommended? For example, can periodic postings be temporarily stopped and executed after SIL completion, or are additional reconciliation or adjustment activities required?

Finally, has anyone successfully completed SIL with RE-FX company codes in scope? We would particularly appreciate any experience regarding project sequencing, alternative approaches, or relevant SAP Notes and official documentation.

Thank you in advance for sharing your experience.

entry.title: SAP‑RPT‑TS: SAP's new Time Series Foundation Model
entry.content:
1. Introduction

SAP has released a new Time Series Foundation Model, SAP‑RPT‑TS. Its key features are:

  • Zero‑shot forecasting: pre‑trained and ready to use, no algorithm selection, no parameter tuning, no series analysis, just forecast.
  • Small, fast, and accurate: ~28M parameters, lightweight and CPU‑friendly, with strong benchmark results.
  • Relational data + covariates: supports multiple targets and past and future covariates of different data types, and provides point forecasts, quantiles, and prediction intervals.
  • Unique capabilities: multi‑target cross‑learning, horizons of up to 1024 steps, and massive multi‑series forecasting (tens of thousands of series, e.g. product × store).
  • Two ways to run: on SAP AI Core or in the SAP HANA Cloud database.

Why we built it. Time‑series forecasting is a constant need across SAP applications: demand planning, inventory optimization, financial and operational planning, and more. Traditionally, each of these use cases needs its own model, trained and maintained separately. SAP‑RPT‑TS removes that overhead: as a foundation model it forecasts zero‑shot, so a new series can be predicted without any training. It is deliberately designed for CPU execution (cost‑effective, no GPU required) and runs both inside SAP HANA Cloud and on SAP AI Core, keeping data within your boundary.

How it works. SAP‑RPT‑TS is pre‑trained on tens of terabytes of time‑series data that mirror the patterns typical of SAP business scenarios. Given historical observations and optional covariates, it returns point forecasts and prediction intervals for each forecast step. 

This blog post focuses on getting you started quickly: Section 2 presents benchmark results; Section 3 shows how to use each deployment option.

 

2. Evaluation and benchmarks

These results come from SAP’s internal evaluations on FEV-Bench and GIFT-Eval using each suite’s tasks and metrics. They have not been submitted to the official leaderboards. The notebook runs the SAP‑RPT‑TS evaluations through the SAP AI Core REST API.

Leading accuracy on FEV‑Bench. FEV‑Bench is a realistic time‑series forecasting benchmark of 100 tasks across 7 real‑world domains, with a deliberate emphasis on exogenous covariates (static, known‑dynamic, and historical‑dynamic). SAP-RPT-TS achieves the lowest mean absolute scaled error (MASE), about 1.41, and the lowest scaled quantile loss (SQL) among the models shown in Fig. 1.

Fig.1. Fev‑Bench: MASE (left) and SQL (right); lower is better

First‑tier on GIFT‑Eval. GIFT‑Eval is a general evaluation suite for zero‑shot forecasting with time‑series foundation models, spanning 23 datasets, 7 domains, and 10 sampling frequencies, and assessing univariate and multivariate forecasting across short/medium/long horizons. In Fig. 2, SAP-RPT-TS ranks near the top on MASE and continuous ranked probability score (CRPS), with a substantially smaller model than the leader.

Fig.2. GIFT‑Eval: MASE (left) and CRPS (right); lower is better

Small model, low inference latency. In this comparison, SAP-RPT-TS has the fewest parameters, about 28 million, and one of the lowest inference latencies (Figs. 3 and 4). Compared with models that run from hundreds of millions to billions of parameters and are several times slower, it reaches comparable accuracy at significantly lower cost. For enterprise forecasting over thousands of series that must be recomputed frequently, this combination of "small size + low latency + high accuracy" translates into a significant total‑cost‑of‑ownership (TCO) advantage.

Fig.3. Inference latency in seconds.

 

Fig.4. Model size, measured by parameter count

 

 

3. Getting started

The examples use a synthetic dataset with 365 daily observations for one building. The target is energy_consumption_kwh, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). The covariates are:

  • Future covariates: temperature_c, humidity_pct, solar_irradiance_kwh_m2, wind_speed_ms, is_weekend, and is_holiday. Their values are supplied for the forecast horizon. Calendar values are known in advance; the example assumes weather values are also available. For production forecasts, supply weather forecasts available at prediction time.
  • Past covariate: occupancy_rate, supplied only for the historical period and set to NULL for the forecast horizon in the PAL input table.

We hold out the final 14 days for forecasting. In the PAL input table, their target values are set to NULL, while future covariates remain populated. Both deployment options use the same dataset; the REST request separates historical observations from future covariates. Fig. 5 shows the first three rows of the input table.

Fig.5. The first three rows of the input table

 

 

Path one: SAP HANA Cloud PAL (in‑database)

If your data is in SAP HANA Cloud, HANA Predictive Analysis Library (PAL) lets you run forecasts directly in the database.

Prerequisites: access to SAP HANA Cloud with PAL enabled. The snippets below come from the linked sample notebook. 

The model supports multiple targets, but the QRC 3/2026 PAL TSFM operator accepts one target column per call, with optional covariates. For joint forecasting of multiple targets, use the SAP AI Core REST API. PAL support is planned for QRC 4/2026.

Prepare a table with an ordering column (ID or timestamp), one target column, and optional covariate columns. Sort the observations by the ordering column, then append one row per forecast step with the target set to NULL. Each series can contain up to 8,192 historical observations, with a forecast horizon of up to 1,024 steps.

SQL example, with history and future rows supplied in one call:

-- TSFM_ENERGY_TBL: target ENERGY_CONSUMPTION_KWH is NULL for the final 14 rows.
-- Future covariates have values for all 14 forecast steps.
-- Past covariate is NULL over horizon.

DO BEGIN
  DECLARE emptyModel TABLE (id INTEGER, value NVARCHAR(5000));

  DECLARE params TABLE (
    PARAM_NAME   NVARCHAR(256),
    INT_VALUE    INTEGER,
    DOUBLE_VALUE DOUBLE,
    STRING_VALUE NVARCHAR(5000)
  );

  params = SELECT 'OUTPUT_PREDICTION_INTERVAL' AS PARAM_NAME, 1 AS INT_VALUE, NULL AS DOUBLE_VALUE, NULL AS STRING_VALUE
  FROM DUMMY
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'CONFIDENCE_LEVEL', NULL, 0.9, NULL
  FROM DUMMY
  UNION ALL
  SELECT 'PIPELINE', NULL, NULL, '{"TSFM": {"args": {}, "inputs": {"data": "ROWDATA"}}}'
  FROM DUMMY;

  data = SELECT "ID", "energy_consumption_kwh", "temperature_c", "humidity_pct",
                "solar_irradiance_kwh_m2", "wind_speed_ms",
                "is_weekend", "is_holiday", "occupancy_rate"
         FROM TSFM_ENERGY_TBL
         ORDER BY "ID";

  CALL _SYS_AFL.PAL_PIPELINE_PREDICT(:data, :emptyModel, :params, result, stat);

  SELECT * FROM :result;
END;

With the Python Machine Learning Client for SAP HANA (hana-ml), run the same forecast with Pipeline.predict:

from hana_ml.algorithms.pal.pipeline import Pipeline
# SAP-RPT-TS is exposed as the TSFM pipeline operator. 
# skip_fit=True uses the pretrained model without fitting it to this dataset.
# hdf: the input table containing history and future rows with NULL targets.
# COVARIATES: all covariate columns; only future covariates have horizon values.
pipe = Pipeline(pipeline={'TSFM': {'args': {}, 'inputs': {'data': 'ROWDATA'}}})
result = pipe.predict(data=hdf, key='ID', exog=COVARIATES, skip_fit=True, output_prediction_interval=1, confidence_level=0.9)
forecast = result.collect()

Reading the result: the output table gives, for each future time point, the point forecast (forecast column), the lower/upper confidence bounds (lower/upper columns). To forecast thousands of series in one go, switch to the Massive variant (MassivePipeline / PAL_MASSIVE_PIPELINE_PREDICT), which processes them in parallel by group key.

Fig. 6 shows the 14-day forecast for IDs 352 through 365. Fig. 7 compares it with recent history and held-out actual values.

Fig.6. Result table.

 

Fig.7. Forecast plot

 

 

Path two: SAP AI Core (REST interface, as a service)

SAP‑RPT‑TS is also available through generative AI Hub in SAP AI Core under the model name sap‑rpt‑ts. Use this path when you call from an application or service, or when your data is outside SAP HANA Cloud. Send a POST request to $DEPLOYMENT_URL/predict to generate probabilistic forecasts for one or more series.

Prerequisites: in AI Core, create a deployment configuration with executableId aicore-sap and model name sap‑rpt‑ts, start the deployment, and retrieve the deployment URL. Include both an Authorization: Bearer $AUTH_TOKEN header and an AI-Resource-Group header in every request. See the SAP-RPT-TS documentation for setup instructions and the sample notebook for the complete example. 

The following is the request payload for the energy consumption example:

payload = {
    "horizon": 14,
    "data": [{
        "timestamp": hist["date"].dt.strftime("%Y-%m-%d").tolist(),
        "target":    [hist["energy_consumption_kwh"].tolist()],
        "past_covariates":   {c: hist[c].tolist() for c in COVARIATES},
        "future_covariates": {c: fut[c].tolist()  for c in FUTURE_COVARIATES},
    }],
    "options": {"confidence_interval": 0.9},
}
out = client.rest_client.post(
    path=_predict_path, body=payload, convert_body_to_camel_case=False
)

The request requires horizon and data; each item in data must include historical target values in target. The timestamp field is optional but recommended. Supply historical covariate values in past_covariates and values available over the forecast horizon in future_covariates. Set options.confidence_interval to request a prediction interval; 0.9 specifies a 90% interval.

Response (excerpt):

{
  "result": [[[528.6, 548.9, 535.9, ...]]], // [n_series][n_variates][horizon]
  "confidence_interval_output": [[[[496.98, 513.8, 503.0, ...],// [n_series][n_variates][2][horizon]
                                    [561.05, 579.4, 564.6, ...]]]],  //   index 0 = lower, 1 = upper
  "result_timestamp": [["2023-12-18", "2023-12-19", "2023-12-20", ...]],
  "detected_interval":         [{"unit": "day", "value": 1}],
  ......  
}

The response contains the following fields. The result[series][variate][step] is the point forecast; confidence_interval_output[series][variate][0 or 1][step] gives lower/upper bounds; result_timestamp holds the forecast timestamp; detected_interval is the automatically detected sampling period. 

 

4. Summary

SAP-RPT-TS delivers accurate, probabilistic forecasts out of the box, with no per-use-case training and a small, CPU‑friendly footprint. Use PAL to forecast directly in SAP HANA Cloud, or the SAP AI Core REST API to integrate forecasting into applications and services. Start with the sample notebooks, then explore covariates and forecasting across multiple series.

 

References

  1. HANA Cloud  PAL : TSFM
  2. Python Machine Learning Client for SAP HANA : TSFM Pipeline Operator
  3. SAP AI Core : SAP‑RPT‑TS
  4. Sample notebooks
  5. FEV-Bench paper 
  6. GIFT-Eval paper

entry.title: SAP Lifecycle Automation ● AI: New SAP, New Ways of Working
entry.content:
SAP transformation has changed. Has the way we deliver it?

🕰️ New SAP → Old ways of working?
🚀 Today’s AI → New ways of working!

SAP transformations are designed to modernise businesses.

We redesign processes.
We modernise architectures.
We migrate data.
We introduce new technology.
We change how organisations operate.

Yet the transformation project itself can still contain large amounts of manual, repetitive and disconnected work.

This raises a simple question:

If AI is changing how businesses operate, shouldn't it also change how SAP transformations are delivered?

This is the starting point for SAP Lifecycle Automation ● AI.

From task automation to lifecycle automation

Automation in SAP projects is not new.

Individual activities can be automated, scripts can execute repeatable operations, testing can be automated, pipelines can move software, and specialised tools can improve individual parts of a transformation.

But automating individual tasks is different from thinking about automation across the lifecycle.

The bigger opportunity is to connect automation and AI across transformation phases:

🔵 Design ● AI
→ 🟣 Build ● AI
→ 🟠 Deploy ● AI
→ 🟢 Run ● AI

Instead of asking:

“Which task could we automate?”

we can ask:

“How could intelligence and automation support the complete lifecycle?”

That changes the perspective.

Design ● AI

Every transformation starts with understanding.

Processes, requirements, architecture, existing systems, data, dependencies and business objectives need to be turned into a transformation design. AI creates an interesting opportunity to support this knowledge-intensive phase. The goal is not simply to produce documents faster. The bigger opportunity is to make transformation knowledge more structured, connected and reusable as the programme moves forward.

Design should create intelligence that Build can use.

Build ● AI

Build translates transformation decisions into working solutions. Configuration, development, integrations, data transformation, testing assets and documentation all create information that can potentially support further automation. Instead of treating every activity as an isolated task, we can increasingly ask:

What can be generated, validated, reused or intelligently supported using what we already know?

And more importantly:

What knowledge created during Build should automatically flow towards Deploy?

Deploy ● AI

Deployment brings together many previously separate streams. Solutions, data, tests, environments, cutover activities, documentation and organisational readiness must converge towards production. Automation has obvious value here, but AI adds another dimension: the possibility of using accumulated lifecycle information to support analysis, preparation and decision-making.

The concept therefore becomes larger than automating a deployment task.

Deploy should consume the intelligence created during Design and Build.

Run ● AI

Go-live should not be the end of lifecycle intelligence. Production operations create another stream of valuable information: incidents, changes, usage, performance, process behaviour and improvement opportunities. That information can help the organisation operate the environment, but it can also become input for the next transformation cycle.

This turns the lifecycle from a sequence into a learning loop:

Design → Build → Deploy → Run → Improve

The real opportunity: connect the lifecycle

This is why the discussion around AI in SAP should be broader than individual AI use cases. The individual use cases matter. But their value can become greater when they form part of a connected lifecycle.

Task Automation

Task
↓
Automation
↓
Result

compared to

Lifecycle Automation ● AI

🔵 Design ● AI
↓
🟣 Build ● AI
↓
🟠 Deploy ● AI
↓
🟢 Run ● AI
↺
Continuous learning and improvement

The shift is therefore not simply:

Manual → Automated

It is potentially:

Disconnected → Connected
Repetitive → Reusable
Reactive → Intelligent
Task automation → Lifecycle automation

Where do you see the biggest opportunity for AI and automation in SAP transformations today?

Design? Build? Deploy? Run?

Or is the bigger opportunity actually connecting all four?

entry.title: SAP Test Automation Services: Five Generations Leading to Autonomous AI Agents
entry.content:
The SAP Test Surface Map

An SAP landscape presents several test surfaces, each with a different automation pattern and a different opportunity for AI-assisted quality engineering.

SurfaceHow Automation EngagesWhere AI Ads Value
SAP GUIGUI scripting drives transaction-based flowsTurning recordings into reusable steps and generating data variations
Fiori / UI5Control IDs and OData-backed viewsRe-anchoring locators after UI changes through self-healing
OData, BAPI, RFCContract-level calls that run quicklyGenerating payload variants from service metadata
IDocs and CPI iFlowsMessage-level validation across systemsComparing mappings and tracing messages end to end
Background jobs and outputScheduled runs with spool and output checksComparing results across runs and releases
Roles and authorizationsRole-based access checksBuilding access test matrices from role design

SAP functional testing typically centers on the business-facing surfaces, while SAP integration testing services extend across the interfaces connecting SAP with banks, logistics partners, data warehouses and other enterprise systems. Authorizations also deserve a dedicated place in the strategy, as role changes frequently accompany application and process updates.

One Change, Five Generations

Consider a new surcharge condition type added to sales order pricing alongside a release upgrade. The change touches Fiori order entry, pricing, billing, output documents, an IDoc sent to a logistics partner and revenue postings in Finance.

The five generations form one sequence: Execute → Reuse → Connect → Assist → Orchestrate

Generation 1 (Execute): Scripted Automation

A recorded script creates a sales order and checks the confirmation. When the surcharge enters the process, an engineer adds the required steps and validations to the affected scripts. The team determines which scenarios should run as part of the release.

  • Automation decides: how to perform recorded steps.
  • Team decides: scope, updates and interpretation.
  • Evidence produced: execution logs and screenshots.

Generation 2 (Reuse): Framework-Driven Automation

The flow is divided into reusable components such as Create Sales Order, Post Goods Issue and Create Billing Document. Customer, material and pricing inputs are maintained through structured data sets.

The surcharge requires one component update plus new rows in the pricing data table, and every scenario using that component inherits the change. This reusable architecture is what allows SAP regression testing services to scale across hundreds or thousands of scenarios.

  • Automation decides: how components are assembled and how data varies.
  • Team decides: scope, component design and interpretation.
  • Evidence produced: structured results per component and data variant.

Generation 3 (Connect): Continuous SAP Testing

The change record now triggers the testing workflow. SAP Cloud ALM supports the preparation of manual and automated tests and their orchestration across test types and automation providers, with test plans connected to requirements and business processes.

For the surcharge change, the sales order regression plan runs when the transport reaches the test system, and the results connect back to the requirement that introduced the change. Testing becomes part of the release flow itself, with traceability across requirements, processes and results.

  • Automation decides: when tests run and where results are recorded.
  • Team decides: which test plans a given change triggers.
  • Evidence produced: traceable results linked to requirements and processes.

Generation 4 (Assist): AI-Assisted SAP Testing

The same surcharge requirement now becomes a source of testing ideas.

AI can draft scenarios around a zero-value surcharge, a maximum-value surcharge, foreign currency orders, partner-specific pricing and credit memos that reverse the surcharge. If the release also redesigns the Fiori order-entry screen, self-healing capabilities can identify new locator candidates and re-anchor the affected tests for engineer review.

The SAP ecosystem has already begun putting these capabilities into practice. In May 2026, Tricentis announced AI-assisted test case generation in SAP Enterprise Continuous Testing by Tricentis, including natural-language test creation, quality agents for scenario design and optimization, and self-healing capabilities.

  • Automation decides: candidate test cases, locator updates and groupings of flagged results.
  • Team decides: approvals, scope and release readiness.
  • Evidence produced: generated assets with approval records.

Generation 5 (Orchestrate): Agentic SAP Testing

Now the change arrives with a broader objective: confirm that the Order-to-Cash process behaves as intended with the new surcharge in place.

An agentic workflow could:

  • Read the change record and requirement, then map them to affected processes in the process hierarchy.
  • Check usage data for the order types, sales organizations and output channels the business actually uses.
  • Select regression scenarios across GUI, Fiori, API and IDoc surfaces, generate cases for uncovered surcharge paths and prepare test data.
  • Trigger execution across automation providers.
  • Group flagged results, trace each group to a likely cause and propose a retest scope.
  • Assemble an evidence pack for release approval.

The usage-based reasoning in step two builds on an approach already present in SAP's Release Assessment and Scope Dependency tool, which identifies Day 1 upgrade impacts based on each customer's usage.

  • Automation decides: scope, generation, data, execution, grouping and the proposed next action.
  • Team decides: critical scope approvals, business acceptance and release sign-off.
  • Evidence produced: a complete decision trail.

What an SAP Testing Agent Reads

An agent's effectiveness depends on the context available to it. In an SAP landscape, different sources answer different testing questions.

Context SourceQuestion It Answer
Process hierarchy and requirements in SAP Cloud ALMWhich business processes does this change touch?
Change records and transportsWhat exactly changed, and where?
Usage dataWhich process variants does this business actually run?
Release notes, What's New and RASD outputWhat did SAP change in this release?
Historical test resultsWhich scenarios have caught issues in this area before?
Test data landscapeWhich data sets are valid for each scenario?

This is what context-aware testing looks like in practice. An agent that can connect process structure with actual usage can shape its testing scope around the way the enterprise operates.

The Delegation Ladder: Calibrating Autonomy

Autonomy works best when it is introduced deliberately, with clear expectations at each level.

LevelWhat the system doesApproval modelTypical SAP use
ExecuteRuns assigned testsTeam assigns every runStable regression packs
RecommendProposes scope, test cases or fixesTeam approves each proposalNew requirements, UI changes
Act with approvalPrepares the full run and waits for sign-offOne approval per cycleRelease upgrade regression
Act and reportRuns, analyzes and reportsTeam reviews afterwardMonthly update cycles
Act within policyOperates inside defined policiesTeam governs the policyHigh-frequency, low-impact changes

Processes can sit at different levels at the same time. A master data maintenance flow might operate at Level 5, while period-end close remains at Level 2.

Human judgment continues to have a clear role in business acceptance, financial controls and release sign-off.

The World Quality Report 2025–26 found that 89% of organizations surveyed are piloting or deploying Gen AI-augmented quality engineering workflows, with 37% in production and 15% at enterprise scale. A clear delegation ladder gives teams a practical structure for expanding these capabilities with defined levels of control.

Evidence as a First-Class Output

For SOX-governed and validated SAP environments, the quality of the evidence matters alongside the test result.

A complete evidence pack records:

  • the inputs the agent read
  • the scope it selected and why
  • the tests it ran or generated
  • the results and how they were grouped
  • the human approvals at each checkpoint

Together, these records provide a reconstructable trail for a testing decision long after the release has passed.

Choosing SAP Automated Testing Tools by Capability

SAP automated testing tools can be evaluated by the capability they bring to a particular part of the landscape.

NeedCapability to look forWhere it exists in the SAP ecosystem
Standard S/4HANA Cloud processesSAP-delivered automations for best-practice processesTest automation for SAP S/4HANA Cloud
Orchestration and traceabilityTest plans across providers, linked to processesSAP Cloud ALM
Browser-based SAP applicationsCloud execution with distributed agentsTricentis Test Automation for SAP
GUI and Fiori with AI generationAgentic test design and self-healingSAP Enterprise Continuous Testing by Tricentis
Non-SAP legs of the processOpen APIs into the orchestration layerCloud ALM test automation APIs

SAP's ALM platforms provide test management and orchestration while supporting integration with third-party test automation providers, allowing organizations to align tools with their landscape and testing requirements.

Where to Start: A Practical Prioritization Model

SAP test strategy services often begin with a simple question: which scenarios should be automated first?

A practical prioritization model is:

Automation priority = Frequency × Business Criticality × Repeatability × Stability

Score each factor from 1 to 5, producing a range from 1 to 625. This is a prioritization aid rather than a statistical model.

ScenarioFBCRSScoreDirection
Standard sales order to billing5554500Automate first, move toward Level 4
Vendor invoice posting with 3-way match5454400

Automate reply

Quarterly intercompany reconciliation253390AI-assisted design, human-led review
Newly introduced subscription billing242116Exploratory testing led by business experts

High-scoring scenarios can form the regression backbone. Mid-range scenarios are strong candidates for AI-assisted design and maintenance, while newer or less stable processes can mature as their automation value becomes clearer.

What a Mature SAP QA Testing Services Engagement Covers

A mature SAP testing services engagement can span five layers:

  • Strategy: prioritization scoring and delegation levels by process
  • Engineering: reusable components across all six test surfaces
  • Continuous quality: regression, functional, integration and authorization testing aligned with release cadence
  • AI augmentation: generation, self-healing, result grouping and impact-based selection
  • Governance: evidence packs, traceability and approval checkpoints

Bottom Line

The five generations trace a steady expansion of automation's role across the SAP quality lifecycle. With SAP's release cadence fixed and agentic capabilities now in the SAP toolchain, enterprise investment is moving toward orchestration layers, context sources and governance models.

Teams evaluating the best SAP testing services provider for their landscape can anchor the choice in two markers: how delegation levels are set for each business process, and how evidence is produced for each release. Defining both, process by process, is what turns agentic testing into dependable release quality.

entry.title: Introducing SAP Enterprise AI Gateway: Control and Visibility Across Agents, Tools, Models, and APIs
entry.content:
Enterprise AI is entering a new phase. What began with individual models and copilots is evolving into an increasingly interconnected landscape of agents, tools, models, APIs, and enterprise systems working together across business processes and technology boundaries.

For years, enterprise integration has focused on connecting applications, data, APIs, events, and processes. Agentic AI is now a new and critical use case. It adds new participants and new ways for systems to interact, introducing additional points of failure and creating new requirements for how enterprises connect AI, control access, and maintain visibility as AI moves into production.

At SAP TechEd in Berlin, we introduced SAP Enterprise AI Gateway, a premium offering built on SAP Business AI Platform. SAP Enterprise AI Gateway extends SAP’s integration foundation to address the need for a more consistent control layer across diverse AI interactions. It helps organizations connect across heterogeneous AI environments, apply consistent controls across AI interactions, and gain end-to-end visibility as those interactions scale.

 

A new control layer for enterprise AI

As agentic AI becomes embedded into enterprise processes, the interaction landscape becomes more complex and diverse. Agents need to collaborate, access enterprise capabilities, use AI models, and interact across applications and systems that run the business. These interactions span different protocols and execution patterns, adding a new layer of complexity to manage enterprise integration.

At the same time, allowing each new protocol or AI technology to develop as a separate operational environment creates another challenge. Identity configurations, access policies, execution controls, monitoring, and operational processes can quickly become fragmented as the number of agents, tools, models, and connections grows. What enterprises need is a way to support these different interaction patterns without creating another fragmented layer of connectivity, control, and operations.

Our approach is not to force these interactions into a single protocol or technical path. Different interaction types serve different purposes and have different technical requirements.

SAP Enterprise AI Gateway is designed to extend, not replace, the integration foundation enterprises already rely on. It supports different interaction models across agents, tools, models, and APIs while providing a more consistent approach to connectivity, control, and visibility. This allows organizations to leverage and preserve the value of existing APIs, integrations, business processes, and enterprise systems while extending them to support new AI interaction patterns.

Connect across protocols and ecosystems

Organizations have mixed application landscapes, and this is no different when it comes to AI agents. SAP customers use SAP agents alongside custom, partner-built, and third-party agents. They will work with different model providers, connect to MCP servers and enterprise tools, and continue to depend on APIs and integrations built over many years.

SAP Enterprise AI Gateway supports these different interaction patterns without forcing them into a single protocol. A2A enables collaboration between agents. MCP provides a standard way for agents to discover and invoke enterprise tools. Model interfaces connect applications and agents to AI models, while APIs continue to support connections to enterprise applications, services, and business processes. Together, SAP Enterprise AI Gateway brings these interaction paths into one unified offering across agents, tools, models and APIs.

Reuse is a key part of this approach. Organizations do not need to rebuild their integration landscape for agentic AI. Existing APIs and integrations can continue to connect to the systems where business processes execute, while enterprise capabilities can be exposed in forms that agents can consume, including through MCP. This allows organizations to extend what they already have rather than create a separate integration stack for every new agent use case.

The result is a more consistent way to connect agents, tools, models, APIs, and enterprise systems across SAP and third-party environments while building on the integration foundation already in place.

 

Control every interaction

As AI systems become more autonomous, connectivity alone is not enough. Enterprises need confidence that interactions take place within defined boundaries: identities need to be understood, access needs to be authorized, enterprise policies need to be enforced, and enterprise systems and sensitive data need to be protected. These concerns are also reflected in the OWASP Top 10 for LLM Applications, including risks such as excessive agency and sensitive information disclosure.

The design principle is consistency, not technical uniformity. An A2A interaction, an MCP tool invocation, an LLM request, and an API call have different execution requirements, so the exact controls will not always be identical. Rather than managing identity, access, policy, and execution controls separately for each interaction type, SAP Enterprise AI Gateway provides a more consistent control approach across agent, tool, model, and API interactions. Organizations can therefore apply the right controls without treating each interaction type as a separate control domain.

For agents and MCP tools, verification status from SAP AI Agent Hub can confirm whether they are approved for use. An approved MCP tool can then be exposed to permitted consumers and invoked within defined policies. A verified external agent, for example, can access enterprise capabilities once authenticated and authorized. For model interactions, sensitive details in customer orders, such as names, addresses, and payment references, can be masked before the request is sent to an AI model. When the underlying business capability is accessed through an API, established authentication, policy enforcement, rate limiting, traffic management, and monitoring capabilities continue to apply.

What differentiates is that SAP Enterprise AI Gateway is not simply another proxy placed in front of AI traffic. It allows organizations to build on the enterprise integration and API management controls they already use, extending them to the new interaction patterns introduced by agentic AI.

 

Scale with end-to-end visibility

As AI interactions become more distributed, visibility can no longer stop at the boundary of a single protocol. Enterprises need to understand how AI systems behave across the interaction landscape: which agents are accessing which enterprise capabilities, which tools and models are being used, where interactions fail, and how activity moves across AI systems and underlying enterprise services.

SAP Enterprise AI Gateway brings monitoring, logging, auditability, and usage visibility closer to the interaction layer, helping IT and AI platform teams gain greater insight into execution across agents, tools, models, and APIs rather than treating each interaction type as an entirely separate operational environment.

At the same time, execution-time visibility can complement broader lifecycle and inventory views across the enterprise AI landscape. These different perspectives can help organizations understand what exists, what is approved for use, and what is happening when AI systems interact with enterprise resources. Over time, the same foundation can support richer usage and cost-management capabilities as they become available.

 

How it works 

Consider a custom agent supporting a procurement workflow. The agent needs current inventory information from an enterprise system and may also need an AI model to reason over that information before responding to the user.

Without a consistent approach, the agent interaction, tool invocation, underlying enterprise API, and model request can each introduce separate identity configurations, access policies, monitoring mechanisms, and operational processes. As agent deployments scale, managing policies individually becomes increasingly difficult, making a consistent, centralized approach essential.

With SAP Enterprise AI Gateway, each interaction can instead use the technical path appropriate to its purpose while remaining part of a more consistent enterprise control and visibility model. The agent may collaborate with another agent through an A2A interaction. When it needs inventory information, it can discover and invoke an enterprise capability exposed through MCP. That capability can reuse existing APIs and integrations to reach the underlying inventory system rather than rebuilding business logic specifically for the agent. If model reasoning is required, the application or agent can use the model interaction path to access the appropriate AI model.

Not every scenario will use every capability, and these interactions do not necessarily occur as one fixed sequence. A model request may use only the model interaction path, while an external agent accessing an enterprise tool may involve agent and MCP interactions. More complex workflows can combine several paths while maintaining the appropriate controls and visibility across the overall scenario.

 

Learn more about SAP Enterprise AI Gateway

The next phase of enterprise AI will be shaped not only by increasingly capable agents and models, but by how effectively they can work across the systems and ecosystems that enterprises depend on. SAP Enterprise AI Gateway is an important step toward making that interaction layer ready for production at enterprise scale.

Take the next step:

  • Explore SAP Enterprise AI Gateway to learn more about the product, capabilities, and architecture. 
  • Join the SAP TechEd recap webinar for a closer look at the latest capabilities, architecture, and launch updates.

entry.title: V1-V2 Transition: A Consultant's Playbook — Part 3: Making the Move (Execution)
entry.content:
This is Part 3 of a multi-part series on planning and executing an SAP Sales & Service Cloud V1-to-V2 transition.
Part 1 covers the Pre-Assessment, and Part 2 covers the Lite Assessment. This post picks up where those two leave off:
actually running the transition. 

The example in this post follows a Phased Go-Live, because it’s the more complex of the two variants and touches every moving part, from load sequencing and delta transfer to ACL management across both systems. But don’t skip ahead if you’re planning a Single Go-Live: in my opinion, nearly everything described here matters just as much there. Pre-migration activities, the object load sequence, data quality verification, test cycles and post-migration activities apply to both variants.

Same disclaimer as the last two posts: this isn't an official SAP best-practice guide. It's a look into how I personally run a V1-to-V2 transition project, the decisions I make and the reasoning behind them, based on my own experience as a consultant, not a prescribed methodology.

A note on accuracy: everything here screenshots, tool details, sequencing, and referenced documentation reflects a snapshot in time. SAP's tools, product roadmap, and feature set keep evolving, so details may have changed by the time you're reading this. I take no liability for the accuracy of the images and information shown; always verify current specifics with SAP or your own project team.

Setting Up the Transition Project

The Pre-Assessment and Lite Assessment hand me a migration plan, a set of findings, and a T-shirt size but none of that
automatically becomes a running project. Before I touch a single tool, I sit down and ask myself a set of questions, and
depending on the answers, some of them turn into a conversation I need to have again with the customer and with the project
team before we start:

  • What is the customer's actual goal?
  • What business outcome want to be achieved
  • What business outcome do we want to achieve with this project, and can we envision working with 
    an AI-infused platform in the near future? 
  • When does the customer want to go live with SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2?
  • Does the customer have the right skilled team  available for the duration of the transition project?
  • Is there a project organization structure in place, with a corresponding RACI?
  • Does the customer want to use this as an opportunity for a business process transformation?
  • What's the customer's current level of knowledge about SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2?
  • Does the customer simply want a lift-and-shift?
  • Does the customer want to migrate only selected data, and cleanse it beforehand?
  • Are there any satellite projects such as an ERP migration project that impacts the schedules?
  • How complex are the customer's specific extensions, and should they even be migrated at all?
  • Does the customer want to migrate based on business units, going live sequentially, unit by unit?

All of these questions and there are more end up shaping how I set up a V1-to-V2 transition project: how long it takes, which
tools I use during execution, and whether I recommend a Big Bang or a Phased approach.

The Example Scenario: DECEMBER AG

Here's the fictional but representative scenario I'll use for this post. DECEMBER AG is structured around three locations
worldwide Hamburg (Germany), Barcelona (Spain), and London (United Kingdom). All three currently run on the same SAP Sales
and Service Cloud V1 system. Since the company doesn't have the capacity to go live in all three countries at once, they've
chosen a Phased approach, spread across a six-month window. Their system landscape consists of an SAP Sales and Service
Cloud V1 system, an S/4 system, and the newly acquired SAP Sales and Service Cloud V2 system. Based on what we knew going
in, and a typical project Define phase, the following project plan took shape.

The Design/Define Phase

When I plan the Design/Define phase of a transition project together with the project manager,
my usual approach looks like this:

  • Establish the project organization structure
  • Define the RACI
  • Review the scope
  • Evaluate any new requirements that have come up since the assessments
  • Define the project plan and review/create the Transition Activity List
  • Determine the migration approach (Big Bang or Phased) and walk through the pros, cons, and risks of each
  • Introduce the migration tools
  • Run show-and-tell sessions covering the new standard processes


A Note on the Transition Activity List

During a transition, a whole range of activities come up, and they differ by data object. My personal recommendation here always
study the official SAP Data Transfer Tool Help documentation closely first. I start with the general pre-conditions, then go object
by object through everything in my transition scope and check the Help page for the prerequisites, pre-migration activities, and
sequential dependencies specific to that object. Some objects, for instance, recommend loading Accounts, Contacts, and BP
Relations before loading the object itself. Others require an object type mapping to be completed first. And others require a
piece of business configuration to be done in SAP Sales or Service Cloud V2 before the actual data object can be migrated via
the Data Transfer Tool from V1 to V2.

Based on all of that, I build a fresh Migration Activity Plan for every project, structured around three main categories: Pre
Migration Activities, Migration Activities, and Post-Migration Activities.

Pre-Migration Activities

For DECEMBER AG, this category covers the following:

  1. Ensure Admin access to the V2 test system
  2. Verify the V2 system is in an initial state before starting migration
  3. Ensure Admin access to the V1 / C4C test system
  4. Request Data Transfer Tool (DTT) access via an SAP Support incident
     (component LOD-LE-MIG-CNS)
  5. Review the Readiness Check report and confirm which objects
    are Supported / Currently Not Supported / Not Supported
  6. Read the official DTT Help documentation and keep a close eye
     on the objects actually in scope
  7. Review Business Roles & Authorizations, and configure Access Control Restrictions (ACL)

Migration Activities

This category covers the actual scope items I need to migrate with the respective migration tools. Each item generally breaks
down into three sub-categories: Prerequisite, Migration activities, and Post-Migration activities. Take the data object Email
as an example.

Example: Email

Prerequisite:

  • Make sure connected business partners Accounts, Employees, and Contacts already exist in the tenant.
  • The MIME types used for email attachments in SAP Cloud for Customer need to be configured and
    allowed in SAP Sales Cloud V2 and SAP Service Cloud V2 as well.




  • Inline images added as URLs will only display correctly if the corresponding domains are added under
    Content Security Policy (User Menu → Settings → All Settings → System Preferences → Content Security Policy).

 

 

 

Migration activities:

For objects migrated via the Data Transfer Tool, the typical activities look like this (using Email as the example):

  • Execute the transition via DTT
  • Review the data in the source system
  • Review the data in the target system and open the Email workspace for your user and confirm the email
    data actually shows up, then open an individual email and verify the expected content is there

Hint: For objects migrated via Data Workbench instead, the typical activities look different:

  • Export the related data entities via Data Workbench in SAP Sales and Service Cloud V1
  • Configure the needed business configuration in SAP Sales Cloud V2 / SAP Service Cloud V2
    for the related data object
  • Download and prepare the import file for this data object from
    SAP Sales Cloud V2 / SAP Service Cloud V2
  • Import the data records into V2

A few things worth flagging here:

Migrating data via Data Workbench overwrites existing data records. It also affects the "Creation Date" and "Last Update Date"
of whatever object you're importing worth knowing before a customer asks why a record's dates look off after the fact.

As of today, Ticket Category is not yet supported by the Data Transfer Tool (DTT) for data migration, although it is on the DTT
roadmap. Therefore, the recommended approach is to migrate Ticket/Case Categories from V1 to V2 using Data Workbench
(Data IMPEX) as a cutover activity, after switching off the ticket Delta Sync in DTT. This is essential because the V1 Delta
Sync can overwrite categories uploaded directly to V2 via Data Workbench, potentially resulting in the loss of category
assignments for tickets created or modified after the Data IMPEX activity.

If already-closed tickets also need to be updated in V2, a feature flag must be requested via an SAP incident.
Without this feature flag, updating already-closed tickets through Data Workbench is not possible.

Also keep the file-size limitation of the Excel or CSV files used for a Data Workbench migration in mind,
it's easy to hit this limit without realizing it until an import fails.

For objects migrated from S/4 to V2 via SAP's standard integration via SAP BTP Integration in my scenario,
that's Account Hierarchy I follow the standard guide SAP publishes for it: SAP CNS Development documentation.

Post-Migration (Email example):

  • Trigger the post-processing for emails once both emails and tickets have been migrated during the Initial Load.
    For Delta Loads, post-processing is already included.

 

Post-Migration Activities

For DECEMBER AG, this category covers (please note: the following topics and sequence could be different for your own
transition project):

  1. Configuration of Business Roles and Authorizations
  2. Autoflows & Workflow Rules
  3. Validations, Determinations, Dynamic Properties
  4. PDI Solutions & Extensions (custom developments)
  5. Integration setup V2 and SAP Backend System
  6. Configuration of Communication Arrangements in V2
  7. Review/ Configure ID Mapping in V2
  8. Activation of migrated Communication System in V2
  9. Plan & Execute Integration Tests
  10. Mashups
  11. Reporting & Analytics
  12. AI Features & Machine Learning
  13. Security & Identity
  14. Finalization & Cutover

I research all of this fresh for every project and build my own individual Migration Activity Plan out of it none of it is copy-pasted
from the last engagement, because the specifics genuinely change project to project.

Assuming the Define phase has been completed successfully, this moves into the Build phase. The foundation of the Transition
Activity List already exists from the earlier Lite Assessment it just gets reworked and validated again during the Design phase,
against the specifics above.

 

The Migration Approach: What Choosing DTT Actually Means

Say you've decided to run the migration via the Data Transfer Tool. It's worth being clear about what that decision actually
implies, because it comes with real trade-offs:

  • You're migrating data objects Business Partners (Accounts, Contacts, Individual Customers…), Tickets, Leads, Opportunities,
    and so on and in most cases their business configuration too (Ticket Types, Account ABC Classification, and similar).
  • You're deliberately minimizing manual effort compared to a Data Workbench migration.
  • You're able to decide in the DTT which key user fields (KUT Field) and extension fields get automatically migrated
    for each object, rather than manually rebuilding them the way you would with Data Workbench.
  • You're deliberately keeping the same IDs for the data objects that they had in V1.
  • You're accepting that the tool transitions data for all regions together there's no way to transfer only a specific
    subset of a selected object. After the Initial Load, further changes sync through a Delta Load that pushes V1 changes
    into V2, but there's no sync in the other direction: changes made directly in V2 can be lost
    if the same record gets modified in V1, because V1 updates always win.
  • You're deliberately ruling out migrating a pre-filtered or hand-selected set of records,
    since the DTT doesn't support that directly. Yes, there's technically a "Test Data Load"
    function that lets you migrate a single record but whether that's realistically usable at scale,
    say against a million Accounts, is something I personally doubt.

A Word of Caution on Data Cleansing

If a customer insists on running data cleansing before migration and tries to press the migration tool into service as a cleansing
tool, my honest recommendation is to steer them elsewhere: either migrate via Data Workbench instead, or if there's a clear
system of truth, say S/4,  for Business Partners consider whether a standard integration makes more sense.

Single Go-Live vs. Phased Go-Live

The Data Transfer Tool offers two migration variants, and it's worth understanding both before picking one:

Single Go-Live moves all your data from V1 to V2 in one go. V1 stays available afterward purely for reference how long depends
on your own content security/retention policy and from that point on, V2 is where all records live going forward.

Phased Go-Live also involves transferring all data from V1 to V2. The key difference compared to a Single Go-Live is that read
and write authorizations for the different business units (BUs) must be managed across both instances using Access Control and
Authorization.

During the transition, V2 acts as a shadow of V1. Depending on the respective go-live phase, each BU works either in V1 or in V2.


Example Phased Go-Live Approach for December AG


Phased Go-Live: The Fine Print

A few details matter a lot here, and they're easy to miss if you're only skimming the tool documentation:

  • All data will be migrated in the initial load, with delta sync running by default all the way through to the final phase. V1 stays
    the system of record for master data throughout, and access control has to guarantee that no master data can be created
    or updated directly in V2 until that final phase of each migration. If V2 users genuinely need to create or update master
    data before then, the user need to create or update the Master Data record in V1. Delta flow only ever runs V1 → V2, never
    the reverse, and there's no legitimate workaround using S/4HANA or another ERP system in between to push V2 changes
    back into V1.
  • The Data Transfer Tool moves every supported object in full, filtering within a selected object isn't possible, and archived
    data from SAP Sales and Service Cloud V1 is excluded entirely.
  • You manage a phased go-live using Access Control Restrictions (ACL). If it's country- or region-based, you apply ACL to the
    specific objects.
  • If you're integrated with SAP S/4HANA or ECC, it's strongly recommended to keep V1 as the master data system of record
    for the duration, edit master data in V1 only, not in V2, to avoid conflicts with the three-way sync between V1, S/4, and V2.
  • Make sure ACL is enabled in both V1 and V2 to actually prevent data conflicts, not just in the system you're phasing into.

For DECEMBER AG, that plays out like this once Germany goes live first: Germany-based employees get edit access in V2,
scoped to German Accounts and Sales Orders, and restricted (read-only or no) access to V1. Spain and UK employees, still
running on V1 at that point, keep their existing V1 access but are restricted from touching German data, and have no access to V2
at all yet. That split is what keeps Germany's business managed exclusively in V2 once it's live, without Spain or the UK
accidentally stepping on it.

For Phase Go-Live approach you need to restrict read and write access of all your scope items.

Restrict read and write access to the scope items in V2

Restrict read and write access to the scope items in V1

 

What to Watch Out for With the Phased Approach

My personal opinion: a Phased approach isn't meant to drag a migration project out indefinitely.
A few reasons why I hold that view:

  • Global reporting. The DTT only transfers data one way, V1 to V2, because DTT is a migration tool and not an integration
    setup that could allow 2 way sync - there's no sync back to V1. So until every country has moved, you either need to feed
    both V1 and V2 data into a reporting tool separately, or open V2 access more broadly and restrict those users to the
    relevant embedded SAC reports.
  • A global view of individual customers or globally managed transactions. Same one-way limitation applies here: if a
    global team is working on the same Account or Contact, whatever gets entered in V1 will overwrite what a V2-only user
    entered, because changes in V2 never sync back to V1.
  • Business configuration. Changes to business configuration in V2 shouldn't be made manually while the migration is still in
    progress, in my case, until the last country has gone live. Business configuration has to be migrated separately
    through the DTT  it isn't part of the tool's Delta function.

Where This Leaves Us

That covers how I set up a transition project during the Design/Define phase, and what actually goes into choosing and
understanding a migration approach Single Go-Live vs. Phased Go-Live, and everything the Phased approach demands in terms
of ACL, delta handling, and discipline around master data. For DECEMBER AG, this is the groundwork Germany's go-live is built
on, with Spain and the UK following in the months after.

About Extensions…

One thing worth being clear about: the Data Transfer Tool covers standard processes and standard objects, including custom
fields, but not the logic behind them. Custom logic, PDI solutions and other extensions need their own migration path. A
colleague of mine is currently working on a dedicated blog about exactly that: how to move your extensions from V1 to V2 using
CCTT and CBOM. I’ll link it here as soon as it’s published, so stay tuned.

If you missed them, Part 1 covers the Pre-Assessment and Part 2 covers the Lite Assessment.

This post reflects my personal approach and experience as a consultant, and does not represent official SAP guidance. It is a
snapshot in time screenshots, tool details, and referenced documentation may no longer be current, and I accept no liability for
their accuracy. Feedback and differing perspectives are very welcome in the comments.

entry.title: AI-Assisted Metrics Trend Analysis in SAP Analytics Cloud
entry.content:
Turning data subscriptions into intelligent analysis

Data is most valuable when it tells a story. Yet for many business users working in SAP Analytics Cloud, the metrics report subscription workflow has historically been a stream of numbers, delivered by email or notification on schedule, accurate and timely, but requiring manual interpretation to uncover what those numbers actually mean over time.

That changes with AI-Assisted Metrics Trend Analysis. Now generally available as of Q4 2026, this Generative AI-powered feature automatically layers natural-language trend analysis on top of your scheduled metrics reports , so every recipient understands not just what the current value is, but how it has been moving over time.

From subscription to insight — automatically

The feature integrates directly into the existing SAC metrics report subscription workflow. There are no separate dashboards to configure, no additional data pipelines to build. Here is the end-to-end flow:

1. Enable AI-Assisted Metrics Trend Analysis on your subscription

Open any metrics report subscription in SAP Analytics Cloud and check the AI Trend Analysis checkbox in the subscription settings. Add this feature whenever you want AI-assisted insights about the historical performance of your metrics or thresholds.

2. AI analyses historical metric performance

At each scheduled send time, the LLM reads the historical snapshot data captured by previous report runs. It describes how KPIs have behaved over time, identifies the most significant variations, and builds a contextual picture of performance trends, using the data your subscription already collects, nothing extra.

3. Natural-language summary is generated

Using that analysis, the system produces a concise analysis that accompanies the report. The summary highlights key changes. For example, a consistent upward trend in revenue KPIs, a sudden dip in customer satisfaction scores, or an acceleration in operational throughput,  framing them in business-relevant language rather than raw percentages.

4. Insight is delivered via email with the scheduled report

The AI-generated trend analysis is embedded directly in the email that subscribers already receive. Today, email is the delivery channel for SAC AI-Assisted Metrics Trend Analysis,  meaning recipients get both the metrics data and its natural-language interpretation in a single, cohesive message in their inbox, with no extra steps or logins required.

Important — two things to know before enabling

  • Minimum 3 reports required: The AI-assisted metrics trend analysis can generate meaningful trend analysis starting from the 3rd report that is sent. Earlier sends will not yet produce a trend analysis, the feature needs a baseline of historical snapshots first.
  • Email only (current scope): This feature is currently only available in report emails. Other delivering channels are planned for the future releases.

Activation of this AI-Assisted feature:

The official SAP documentation provides a step-by-step guide to activating this feature in your SAP Analytics Cloud tenant.  This is a base AI-feature offered free of charge.

Outlook

AI-Assisted Metrics Trend Analysis reflects a broader shift in how SAP Analytics Cloud is evolving: from a platform that surfaces data to one that actively interprets it for you. entry.title: Авторизації в SAP: чому неправильний доступ = фінансовий ризик
entry.content:
Управління доступом у SAP — тема, яку часто відкладають «на потім» і яка потім обертається аудиторськими зауваженнями, інцидентами безпеки або, в гіршому випадку, реальними фінансовими втратами. Розберімося в базових принципах авторизаційної концепції SAP і найпоширеніших помилках.

Як влаштована авторизаційна система SAP

В основі авторизацій SAP лежить концепція об'єктів авторизації. Кожна дія в системі (переглянути документ, змінити дані, запустити транзакцію) захищена одним або кількома авторизаційними об'єктами з конкретними значеннями полів. Ролі (Roles) — це контейнери, що об'єднують набір авторизацій для певної функції. Профілі (Profiles) генеруються з ролей автоматично і присвоюються користувачам.

Одинарні та композитні ролі

  • Single Role - роль для конкретної функції (наприклад, «Перегляд замовлень на купівлю»)
  • Composite Role - об'єднання кількох одинарних ролей для певної посади (наприклад, «Менеджер з закупівель»)
  • Derived Role - роль, успадкована від батьківської з різними значеннями організаційних рівнів (різні підрозділи, заводи)

Найпоширеніші помилки в авторизаційній концепції

  1. SAP_ALL або надмірно широкі ролі - «тимчасово» дали адміністративний доступ і забули забрати
  2. Відсутність concept Segregation of Duties - один користувач може і створити постачальника, і провести платіж
  3. Авторизації через Development клас замість Production - тестові ролі потрапляють у продуктивну систему
  4. Відсутність регулярного рев'ю доступів - людина змінила роль або звільнилася, але доступ залишився
  5. Wildcard-значення (*) в критичних полях - надає доступ до всіх об'єктів замість конкретних

💡 Практичне правило: авторизаційну концепцію треба проєктувати до початку конфігурації системи, а не після. Ретроспективне виправлення авторизацій у вже запущеній системі — болісний і ризикований процес.

SU53: ваш найкращий друг при помилках доступу

Коли користувач отримує помилку «Немає авторизації», транзакція SU53 показує саме той авторизаційний об'єкт і значення, яких не вистачає. Це відправна точка для будь-якого аналізу авторизаційних проблем. BASIS-адміністратор і консультант повинні знати цей інструмент «на автопілоті».

entry.title: Updating SmartRecruiters Job Fields via API When Position Mapping Is Not Available
entry.content:
The API-Based Workaround

SmartRecruiters exposes a public REST API that allows all five fields to be updated programmatically on any existing job. The workaround design has four steps:

Step 1: Job Created in SmartRecruiters

A job is created (manually, from a Position, or via integration). SmartRecruiters fires the job.created webhook event containing the new job's ID.

Step 2: Webhook Receives the Event

An integration middleware (SAP Integration Suite, BTP, or any HTTP listener) receives the job.created event payload and extracts the job ID.

Step 3: Enrich with Source Data

The middleware looks up the correct values for Industry, Function, Experience Level, Type of Employment, and Location from the source Position or a mapping table.

Step 4: PATCH the Job via SmartRecruiters API

A JSON PATCH call is sent to https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId} with all five field updates in a single request.

API Call Details

PATCH  https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId}

[
  {
    "path": "/industry",
    "op": "add",
    "value": { "id": "airlines_aviation" }
  },
  {
    "path": "/function",
    "op": "add",
    "value": { "id": "administrative" }
  },
  {
    "path": "/experienceLevel",
    "op": "add",
    "value": { "id": "director" }
  },
  {
    "path": "/typeOfEmployment",
    "op": "add",
    "value": { "id": "permanent" }
  },
  {
    "path": "/location",
    "op": "add",
    "value": {
      "countryCode": "us",
      "regionCode": "CA",
      "city": "San Francisco"
    }
  }
]

Tip: Use the SmartRecruiters GET /industries, /functions, /experience-levels, and /types-of-employment endpoints to retrieve all valid picklist IDs for your tenant.

https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/docs/industries

https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/docs/functions

https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/docs/levels

https://developers.smartrecruiters.com/docs/typesofemployment

Screenshot — PATCH Call in API Client

The screenshot below shows the PATCH request body and the 200 OK response returned by the SmartRecruiters API:

Triggering the Integration via Webhook

To make this workaround fully automated, configure a webhook subscription in SmartRecruiters to fire whenever a new job is created. The recommended event is:

Webhook Event:  job.created

The webhook payload includes the job id, which your middleware can immediately use to fire the PATCH call. The screenshot below shows a sample job.created webhook event:

Webhook Configuration Tips

  • Subscribe to job.created in the SmartRecruiters Admin panel under Integrations → Webhooks.
  • Your endpoint should respond with HTTP 200 within the timeout window to acknowledge receipt.
  • Implement idempotency — store processed job IDs to avoid duplicate PATCH calls if the webhook retries.
  • Use GET /jobs/{jobId} to check whether the fields are already set before calling PATCH, to handle re-fires gracefully.
  • This integration can be built on SAP Integration Suite, SAP BTP, or any HTTP-capable middleware.
    Summary -  
  • KBA 3746432 documents that Location, Function, Industry, Experience Level, and Type of Employment cannot currently be mapped from a Position in SmartRecruiters.
  • Manual workaround (without API): Recruiters must manually populate these fields for every job.
  • API solution: A single JSON PATCH call to https://api.smartrecruiters.com/jobs/{jobId} updates all five fields in one request.
  • Automation trigger: Subscribe to the job.created webhook to fire the PATCH call automatically whenever a new job is created — eliminating manual intervention entirely.

entry.title: Zero-shot time series forecasting with SAP-RPT-TS in SAP HANA Cloud and SAP AI Core
entry.content:
SAP is expanding its tabular AI capabilities with updates to the SAP-RPT AI model family, which will help companies harness structured data for faster, more accurate predictions. As part of the SAP Business AI Platform, these innovations provide additional context that supports the ability of AI to reason and take appropriate action.

While large language models (LLMs) are powerful tools for handling unstructured data, they often struggle with the structured data that is critical to everyday business processes and decisions. Tabular AI is designed to handle this kind of data — it enables AI to process, understand, and make predictions using structured data found in business applications, databases, and other sources.

SAP was an early mover in tabular AI with its 2025 launch of the SAP-RPT-1 AI model and continues to bring new models and capabilities to market for AI developers, data teams, and business users.

 

Introducing SAP-RPT-TS: time series forecasting joins the SAP-RPT AI model family

Time series forecasting is now unlocked with the new SAP-RPT-TS tabular foundation model, the latest and key expansion of the SAP-RPT AI model family. Here is what makes it distinct:

  • Pretrained foundation model. SAP-RPT-TS is a Relational Pre-trained Transformer (RPT) model. This removes the need to collect training datasets, manage compute infrastructure, or endure cycles of model experimentation, tuning, monitoring, and retraining.
  • Zero-shot business forecasting. SAP-RPT-TS provides a true zero-shot forecasting experience with no model training or tuning involved. By supplying a snapshot of historical data using in-context learning, the forecast is generated on-the-fly at predict time, enabling predictions across key enterprise indicators such as demand, sales, and operational metrics. It can help answer questions like: How does demand move next month? Where is inventory projected to run short? How does revenue develop across regions going forward?
  • Probabilistic predictions. The model produces forecasts grounded in the provided context data, returning calibrated prediction intervals that quantify uncertainty out-of-the-box, not just point estimates. This reduces the risk of costly over- or under-prediction decisions.
  • Flexible and resilient data handling. SAP-RPT-TS handles a wide range of forecast scenarios: univariate and multivariate series, both past and known-future covariates, and multiple targets with and without cross-learning. It automatically manages gaps and missing values in the series, and detects seasonality, trends, and the influence of covariates to improve accuracy. Support for intermittent time series is already on the roadmap for the next model update.
  • High quality, fast and lightweight. On enterprise data, SAP-RPT-TS yields predictions that are mostly superior to state-of-the-art narrow AI forecast models built specifically for such tasks. It delivers low-latency instant forecasts from within SAP HANA Cloud or SAP AI Core, served from a cost-effective CPU environment, with no expensive GPU hardware required.

 

Consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP HANA Cloud

Developers and business users can immediately access the model through SAP HANA Cloud or SAP AI Core.  To use SAP-RPT-TS directly from the database, first ensure that NLP services are enabled within your HANA Cloud instance configuration, and that the instance is version 2026.28 (Q3 2026) or newer.

In the current release, SAP-RPT-TS is accessible through the TSFM operator for PAL AutoML / Pipeline models (TSFM in hana_ml 2.30). There are two ways to use it. 

  • Use the PIPELINE PREDICT function with the TSFM operator: in skip-fit mode for instant zero-shot time series forecasts:
  • Use the AutoML FIT function with the TSFM operator: which simply allows to use it alongside classic time series operators (ARIMA, BSTS, AMTSA, HGBT-TS, MLR-TS, and others) within the AutoML Time Series scenario, where it is evaluated as a candidate model and selected only when it delivers the best forecast.

 

The screenshot above captures this in practice: a PAL pipeline configured for skip-fit mode, and the resulting output showing calibrated prediction intervals returned alongside the historical series, with no training step required. What stands out is how little code is involved. A handful of lines using hana_ml is all it takes to generate a production-quality time series forecast directly from SAP HANA Cloud.

More details on consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP HANA Cloud can be found in the companion blog post by xinchen   SAP‑RPT‑TS SAP's new Time Series Foundation Model, incl. a sample notebook.

 

Consuming SAP-RPT-TS from SAP AI Core 

SAP-RPT-TS is also available directly through SAP AI Core via the foundation-models scenario. Getting started requires creating a configuration and then a deployment using executableId: aicore-sap and modelName: sap-rpt-ts-1.0, or latest to always reference the newest model version. From there, the model is consumed through standard REST API calls, with no infrastructure to provision and no training jobs to manage. Examples covering a range of forecasting scenarios and input structures are provided in the example payloads documentation 

.

SAP-RPT-TS in SAP Integrated Business Planning for Demand

The first SAP application to integrate SAP-RPT-TS is SAP Integrated Business Planning for Demand (or IBP, generally available in Q1 2027 release update). Planners can use SAP-RPT-TS alongside any other algorithm in statistical forecasting, running it exactly as they do today with any other algorithm and reviewing the results directly in their planning views. No new tool, no exports, no coding.

The demo above shows this experience end-to-end: a planner running SAP-RPT-TS as one of the active forecast methods in IBP, selecting it, running it, and comparing its output against other models within the same familiar interface. The integration is seamless precisely because SAP-RPT-TS fits into existing workflows rather than replacing them.
