entry.title: Give Your AI Agents Long-Term Memory: SAP Agent Memory Service Is Now Generally Available
entry.content:
Every agent session starts from scratch. That has been the reality for most AI agents today. Ask an agent to help you resolve a billing dispute, and it might ask you the same clarifying questions it asked last week, with no recollection of your preferences, your previous decisions, or the work you've already done together. This is not a limitation of the LLM, it is a fundamental gap in how agents are built. Without persistent memory, every interaction starts at zero.

With the General Availability of SAP Agent Memory Service in Q3 2026, that changes.

The Problem: AI Agents That Forget Everything

Enterprises deploying AI agents face a challenge that is easy to overlook but costly in practice: agents are stateless by default. When a session ends, the context ends with it. Preferences, past decisions, in-progress workflows, and the outcomes of previous conversations all disappear.

This creates friction in exactly the scenarios where agents are supposed to save time, for example:

  • A collection agent asks a customer to re-confirm payment preferences it has already captured.
  • An HR assistant forgets that a user prefers documents in German and generates English responses each time.
  • A configuration transport agent has no memory of approvals completed in a previous session, restarting an hours-long workflow from the beginning after a timeout.

Stuffing chat history into the prompt as a workaround is expensive, fragile, and hits context window limits fast. What agents need is not a bigger prompt, they need real, durable memory.

Introducing SAP Agent Memory Service Powered by SAP HANA Cloud

SAP Agent Memory Service is a fully managed, persistent memory layer for AI agents on SAP BTP. It gives agents the ability to store knowledge across sessions, retrieve it semantically when it is needed, and maintain an auditable log of their interactions, all backed by SAP HANA Cloud's vector engine and governed with enterprise-grade retention controls.

Powered by SAP HANA Cloud's built-in NLP capabilities, Agent Memory Service is not just a key-value cache. It is an evolving memory store that allows agents to write what they learn, recall what matters by meaning rather than keyword, and improve over time as memories accumulate. All agent memories and messages are stored directly in your SAP HANA Cloud instance, the same trusted, enterprise-grade database that already powers your business data. so, your agent context lives where your data lives, governed by the same security and compliance controls you already rely on.

SAP Agent memory Service Powered by SAP HANA Cloud (Note - *Planned items 2027)

How It Works

Agent Memory Service stores two types of records:

Memories are durable, semantically searchable knowledge entries - facts, decisions, summaries, and preferences that an agent should recall across future sessions. When an agent writes a memory, the service automatically generates a vector embedding using SAP HANA Cloud's NLP engine. At retrieval time, a vector similarity search surfaces the most relevant memories for the current context, even when the query shares no keywords with the stored content.

Messages are raw, chronological conversation logs grouped by session. They give agents an auditable, replayable record of every interaction - essential for compliance, handovers, and multi-turn context within an active session.

All data is scoped to an (agentID, invokerID) pair, ensuring that memories and messages are isolated per agent and per user, with no cross-contamination between tenants, agents, or users.

The service exposes a standard OData REST API with four key endpoints:

 No proprietary SDK is required. An optional Python client is available via the SAP Cloud SDK for Python for those who prefer it.

What Becomes Possible

Agent Memory Service transforms what an agent can do across three dimensions:

  • Continuity across sessions - A user's preferences, in-progress tasks, and past decisions survive session boundaries. When a user returns, whether hours or weeks later, the agent picks up where they left off. For example - "Customer prefers consolidated invoices" is automatically recalled in every billing cycle, without the user needing to say it again.
  • Leaner, more precise prompts - Rather than appending entire conversation histories to every prompt, agents retrieve only the top-K semantically relevant memories per turn. This keeps prompts lean, reduces LLM costs, and improves response quality.
  • Improvement over time - As memories accumulate and access timestamps update, agents get sharper without retraining. Frequent dispute patterns are recognized and resolved faster. Recurring questions are anticipated and addressed proactively.
  • Human oversight and control - Users can inspect, edit, or delete their memories directly, providing full transparency. Audit teams can trace how a billing decision or dispute was handled, turn by turn, using the message log.

Getting Started

Agent Memory Service is available as a standalone SAP BTP service subscription tied to your SAP HANA Cloud instance (Bring Your Own HANA plan).

Provision via SAP BTP Service Marketplace - In your SAP BTP subaccount, add the hana plan for SAP HANA Cloud and the hana-agent-memory plan as entitlements. Provision an SAP HANA Cloud instance or use your already existing one (make sure to enable "nlp": true in the ‘Advanced Setting’ configuration - this is required for semantic search). Then create an Agent Memory Service instance using the ‘hana-agent-memory’ plan, link it to your HANA Cloud instance, and create a service key. The key gives you the clientid, clientsecret, url, and application_url fields needed to authenticate via OAuth 2.0 client credentials.

Subscribe to 'hana-agent-memory' service plan on SAP BTP Cockpit

 

Call the API directly or use the SAP Cloud SDK for Python - Once provisioned, you can call the OData REST API from any HTTP client. For Python-based agent development, the SAP Cloud SDK for Python provides an optional client that handles authentication and request handling, with ready-to-use patterns for storing memories, running semantic search, logging conversation turns, and managing retention.

For the full step-by-step setup guide, API samples, and best practices, see the SAP Help Portal: Agent Memory Service Guide. The complete API reference and interactive sandbox are available on SAP Business Accelerator Hub.

Conclusion

The journey toward agentic SAP HANA Cloud has been about making agents smarter at every layer, from the data they discover and query, to the context they carry with them over time.

Agent Memory Service addresses the most fundamental limitation in today's agent architectures: the absence of persistent, governed, enterprise-grade memory. With it, agents stop being one-shot tools and become evolving partners.

For developers, this means:

  • A managed, persistent memory layer that works across SAP and non-SAP agent frameworks (LangChain, LangGraph, SAP BAIP, and custom agents)
  • Semantic retrieval powered by SAP HANA Cloud's vector engine, no external embedding service required
  • Native integration in Joule Studio (planned towards 2027) and the SAP Cloud SDK for Python
  • Built-in governance: configurable retention, data isolation, OAuth 2.0 security, and audit logging

With Agent Memory Service now generally available, SAP HANA Cloud continues to establish itself as the database for SAP's AI-native software architecture, not just storing data, but helping agents remember, learn, and improve across every interaction.

Note on availability: The service is currently available on a bring-your-own SAP HANA Cloud model, where you provision and manage your own HANA Cloud instance. A fully managed offering, where SAP handles the underlying infrastructure entirely, with no HANA Cloud instance required on your end, is planned towards the end of 2026. Stay tuned for updates.

entry.title: SAP HANA Cloud Scale-Out: Expanding In-Memory Capacity Beyond Single-Node Limits
entry.content:
As data-driven enterprises grow, so does the demand for in-memory processing at scale. SAP HANA Cloud already offers vertical scaling, increasing the size of a single node instance to accommodate growing workloads. But what happens when your dataset simply outgrows what any single node can hold?

SAP is introducing SAP HANA Cloud scale-out as part of its Multi-Dimensional Elastic Scaling strategy: a solution that extends memory capacity horizontally across multiple nodes, while keeping the full simplicity of working with a single HANA instance.

Scale-Out in Context: SAP HANA Cloud's Multi-Dimensional Elastic Scaling

Scale-out completes a broader, multi-dimensional approach to elasticity in SAP HANA Cloud, where different mechanisms address different needs for in-memory data growth:

 

Scaling dimension

Mechanism

When to use

Vertical

Scale-up

Growing data that still fits on one node

Temporary burst

Elastic Compute Nodes (ECNs)

Predictable workload peaks (e.g. month-end reporting)

Permanent horizontal

Scale-out (planned)

Data volume that permanently exceeds single node capacity

 

What Is SAP HANA Cloud Scale-Out?

SAP HANA Cloud scale-out is a permanent horizontal scaling capability that distributes a single HANA Cloud instance across multiple nodes, one coordinator node and multiple worker nodes operating together as a shared-nothing cluster.

Data including tables and partitions is distributed across all nodes. The coordinator node orchestrates query execution and manages cluster-wide operations, while all nodes participate equally in storing data and processing queries in parallel. Despite this distributed internal architecture, the system presents itself to applications as a single SAP HANA Cloud instance: same SQL interface, same connection endpoint, no application workflow changes required.

 

 

Key Capabilities

Permanent Scaling – breaking the maximum in-memory size limitation of data holding for HANA Cloud instance, enable very large size for high performance compute.

One instance with multiple nodes– data distributed among coordinator and workers, and operate as one internal shared-nothing cluster, yet appear to user as a single large HANA instance behaving identically to a single-node instance.

Online Flexible Scaling – Add worker nodes to expand memory capacity and query concurrency, or remove workers and resize nodes to right-size the instance. Now you can choose the node size and number of workers that best match the memory and CPU requirements of your workload, giving you more flexibility to find the right SAP HANA Cloud configuration. These changes can be performed online and remain transparent to applications, so capacity can evolve with the business without downtime.

Migration Tool Support – Reduce manual effort for migrating existing SAP HANA Scale-Out systems to SAP HANA Cloud by streamlining the migration process.

-------

Exciting innovations are ahead as SAP HANA Cloud continues to pave the way for the agentic future! Make sure to follow the SAP HANA Cloud tag for updates on the latest developments, and check out #whatsnewinsaphanacloud for new blog posts, technical deep dives, and product news.

SAP TechEd 2026 is here, and once again, SAP HANA Cloud is at the center of the action! Building on the innovations introduced at TechEd 2025 and throughout the year, we're continuing to push the boundaries of what's possible with enterprise data and AI. As the Database for Business AI, SAP HANA Cloud provides a powerful foundation for building intelligent applications, connecting business data, and enabling the next generation of AI-driven innovation.

Across the SAP Business AI platform, three layers of contextualization power your AI use cases. The first is the SAP Knowledge Graph, with fifty years of SAP process knowledge, encoded and ready for Joule. The second is SAP Business Data Cloud, delivering governed data products with rich semantics. And the third, uniquely powerful, is a custom knowledge layer built with SAP HANA Cloud: your domain ontologies, your entity relationships, your business context, fully customer-managed, running natively inside SAP HANA Cloud's multi-model engines. By combining graph, vector, and SQL retrieval, SAP HANA Cloud helps AI agents access the enterprise context they need to deliver more accurate, relevant, and actionable results.

And there's much more to discover! From agentic capabilities accessible through Joule to the newly released SAP Agent Memory Service, which enables AI agents to retain context across sessions and workflows, SAP HANA Cloud continues to expand what's possible with Business AI. The new Time Series Foundation Model also brings on-the-fly predictions directly into the database, without requiring model training. With even more innovations on the horizon before the end of 2026, there's plenty to explore at SAP TechEd this year!

Read on to explore all the major announcements from SAP TechEd 2026.

 

SAP HANA Cloud Admin Agent — Now Integrated with Joule

Managing an SAP HANA Cloud instance demands deep expertise: diagnosing memory growth, tracing out-of-memory situations buried in calculation views, navigating multi-step version upgrades at odd hours. The new SAP HANA Cloud Administration Agent brings expert-level operational intelligence directly into these workflows, in natural language. Describe what you need, whether that's understanding why your database is running slow, identifying optimization opportunities, or scaling systems down after business hours, and the agent investigates, diagnoses, and recommends a course of action for you to approve. It is designed for SAP HANA Cloud administrators, DBAs, and cloud operations teams: you don't need to be an SAP HANA expert to get expert-level outcomes, but if you are, the agent handles the administrative groundwork so you can focus on the decisions that matter! Learn more in this blogpost by @jose_at_sap 

 SAP HANA Cloud Administration Agent in Joule

Agent Memory Service

Every AI agent session starts from scratch, and for enterprise deployments, that is a costly problem! Agents re-ask questions already answered, forget user preferences established in previous interactions, and lose track of in-progress workflows after a timeout. With the General Availability of SAP Agent Memory Service in Q3 2026, this fundamental limitation is addressed head-on. Built on SAP HANA Cloud's vector engine, the service provides a fully managed, persistent memory layer for AI agents on SAP Business AI Platform: agents can store knowledge across sessions, retrieve it semantically at the right moment, and maintain a governed, auditable log of their interactions, all within the same trusted SAP HANA Cloud instance that already powers your business data. The result is agents that remember user preferences, pick up workflows where they left off, and grow sharper over time without retraining, while keeping prompts lean and enterprise governance intact. Read this blogpost by @shabana   to explore how it works and how to get started.

Access by Through Joule Studio Runtime (App Fnd) for native in-house SAP developer experience

 

 

Subscription as a stand-alone SAP BTP Service tied to your SAP HANA Cloud instance

 

 

Time Series Foundation Model (RPT-TS)

At SAP TechEd 2026, we're excited to unveil SAP-RPT-TS! A breakthrough time series forecasting foundation model and the newest member of the SAP-RPT AI model family, built to bring enterprise-grade forecasting directly to SAP HANA Cloud. Where traditional large language models fall short on the structured data that drives your business, SAP-RPT-TS is purpose-built for it. It can deliver accurate, zero-shot forecasts for demand, sales, revenue, and inventory with no model training, no tuning, and no data science overhead. Simply supply a snapshot of your historical data, and the model generates production-quality forecasts on the fly, complete with calibrated prediction intervals that quantify uncertainty, so your teams can act with confidence and avoid the cost of over- or under-forecasting. It handles the messy realities of real-world data automatically, from missing values and seasonality to multivariate series, and runs natively within SAP HANA Cloud on cost-effective CPU infrastructure. No expensive GPUs required! Best of all, you can get started in just a few lines of code with hana_ml, or explore it instantly in the RPT Playground. With SAP-RPT-TS, world-class forecasting is now built right into the platform you already trust.

 Try out SAP-RPT-TS via the SAP RPT Playground now

Learn more about our new Time Series Foundation Model in this blogpost by @ChristophMorgen

 

Scale-Out Support for SAP HANA Cloud

SAP HANA Cloud Scale-out is one of the capacity increasing solutions that SAP HANA Cloud will provide for Elasticity & Scalability. It is the permanent horizontal scaling using multiple worker nodes and one coordinator node to work together internally as a shared-nothing cluster system to provide large memory capacity. It is one large-size HANA instance that behaves the same as single node HANA instance.  Beyond addressing the in-memory data size limitations of a single node, scale-out gives customers greater flexibility to find the right SAP HANA Cloud configuration for their specific workload requirements, allowing them to combine multiple nodes to achieve the precise balance of node size and performance class that their workload demands. In a scale-out system, all nodes operate under a main coordinator node, working together to process user queries and tasks. Data, including tables and partitions, is distributed across the nodes, enabling the query optimizer to leverage parallel execution for faster processing of queries involving large tables.

Learn more about Scale-out in this blogpost by @zhen_tian

 

Real-Time Event-Driven Architectures and Agents

with SAP HANA Cloud and SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh

What is smarter than an AI agent? An event-driven AI agent. The standard agent pattern is reactive: a user types, an agent responds. But business reality does not wait for prompts. So, let us make agents event-driven through three phases:

Sense: data crosses a threshold, a process reaches a critical state, something shifts in your landscape. SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh captures these signals (events) the moment they happen, propagating them in real time across your entire landscape, without polling that burns unnecessary compute and tokens.

Contextualize: those events hit a multi-model custom knowledge layer built with SAP HANA Cloud, spanning vector search, knowledge graphs, relational data, and in-database AI. Agents reason over live business data, understanding not just that something changed, but what it means, to respond accurately.

Respond: the right agents are activated through SAP Integration Suite, advanced event mesh, each acting according to its role in the business process with the right business context, with no manual trigger needed.

Data scientists and integration experts collaborate to build and maintain event-driven agentic architectures, keeping business context current within the custom knowledge layer. This includes defining how events map to agent actions and which agents handle which scenarios, enabling use cases from dynamic pricing and fraud detection to supply chain optimization and predictive maintenance. With improved interoperability between SAP HANA Cloud and SAP Integration Suite, Advanced Event Mesh planned for Q4 2026, this capability is only getting sharper.

Exciting innovations are ahead as SAP HANA Cloud continues to pave the way for the agentic future! Make sure to follow the SAP HANA Cloud tag for updates on the latest developments, and check out #whatsnewinsaphanacloud for new blog posts, technical deep dives, and product news.

To dive deeper into recent innovations and latest webcasts, watch our curated YouTube playlist.

Finally, be sure to join the SAP HANA Cloud Community. It's a great place to ask questions about the topics covered at SAP TechEd 2026, learn more about SAP HANA Cloud, and discuss the innovations highlighted in this blog with our experts and fellow community members.

Thank you for being part of the SAP HANA Cloud journey.

We look forward to seeing how you bring these innovations to life and build what matters!

entry.title: UI5 TypeScript development just got smoother
entry.content:
No more @namespace annotations: ui5-tooling-transpile now auto-detects your UI5 namespace

If you write UI5 with TypeScript, you have almost certainly written this in every controller, control, and component:

/**
 * @namespace ui5.ecosystem.demo.myapp
 */
export default class Main extends Controller {

That annotation exists for one reason: the Babel preset that converts your TypeScript class to a classic sap.ui.define call needs to know which namespace prefix to put in front of controller.Main. Without it, the generated module name comes out wrong and the app breaks at runtime.

Starting with ui5-tooling-transpile 3.14.0, you do not need to write it anymore.

What changed

The new version of babel-preset-transform-ui5 (7.11.0) can derive the namespace from the project structure on its own. ui5-tooling-transpile now reads the namespace and source path configuration from your ui5.yaml, builds the sourceFolders map (a table that says "files under webapp/ belong to this namespace"), and hands it directly to the preset before transpilation starts.

The result is that every file in your project picks up the right namespace prefix automatically. You delete the annotations, and the output is identical to what you had before.

Here is what a controller looks like before and after:

// before
/**
 * @namespace ui5.ecosystem.demo.myapp
 */
export default class Main extends Controller {
  onInit(): void {
    // ...
  }
}
// after
export default class Main extends Controller {
  onInit(): void {
    // ...
  }
}

Same output. One annotation fewer per file. In a medium-sized app with a dozen controllers and a handful of controls, that is a meaningful amount of noise gone.

What it covers

The auto-detection works across all three scenarios you are likely to encounter.

App development. The middleware and the build task both read the project's namespace from ui5.yaml. Files under webapp/ (or whatever path you have configured in resources.configuration.paths.webapp) map to that namespace. Nothing to configure.

Library development. For library projects src/ maps to the project namespace. Same automatic derivation, same zero-config experience.

Middleware with a dependency library. This is the case that was missing before and is the main reason the change landed. When your app runs ui5 serve with ui5-tooling-transpile as middleware, and one of your workspace library dependencies also uses ui5-tooling-transpile, the middleware now walks the dependency graph and registers the sourceFolders of each dependency alongside your own. So if a controller from a local library gets served through the middleware, it resolves to my.lib.controller.Shared instead of src.controller.Shared. No annotations needed in the library either.

External Babel configs. If your project supplies a .babelrc, babel.config.js, or similar, the auto-derived sourceFolders is normally not injected because the external config takes over. Add injectSourceFolders: true to your ui5.yaml configuration block for ui5-tooling-transpile and the preset will receive the derived values, with anything already set in your external config taking precedence:

builder:
  customTasks:
    - name: ui5-tooling-transpile-task
      afterTask: replaceVersion
      configuration:
        injectSourceFolders: true

How to upgrade

Update ui5-tooling-transpile to 3.14.0 or later in your project:

npm install ui5-tooling-transpile@latest --save-dev

Then delete the @namespace JSDoc blocks from your TypeScript source files. That's it. If you use an external Babel config and want to stop writing annotations there too, add injectSourceFolders: true as shown above.

The Easy UI5 TypeScript templates have been updated to match, so new projects generated from those templates will start without annotations from the beginning.

Where to find it

The package is on npm:

👉 https://www.npmjs.com/package/ui5-tooling-transpile

It's part of the ui5-ecosystem-showcase, the collection of UI5 CLI extensions the community uses every day. The showcase itself runs without any @namespace annotations now, so the complete set of app and library scenarios there serves as a working reference.

entry.title: How I Connected Claude Code to a Real SAP S/4HANA On-Premise System Using MCP
entry.content:
▶ Watch the full-quality video: https://youtu.be/8ZFwoMb9xrM

One prompt, one MCP tool call, 13 open maintenance notifications from an SAP S/4HANA on-premise test system, and a dashboard built from them.

I connected an AI agent to a real SAP S/4HANA on-premise system through the SAP Cloud Connector and an MCP server on SAP Integration Suite. No ABAP, no inbound firewall ports, no mock services in between: the agent reads maintenance notifications straight from the SAP system and then works with them.

The video above shows the agent turning those notifications into a dashboard. The same MCP server plugs into Claude Code with one command, so once real SAP objects are in a coding agent's context, it can write files, generate code and build things from them.

Scope, up front: this is a feasibility demo, not a production deployment. The backend is a real S/4HANA 2023 on-premise system, but it is a QA/test system loaded with test data I created for this scenario. Nothing here touches production, and the project continues in testing.

Part 3 of a series

Part 1 built the agent, Part 2 moved it to a governed gateway, Part 3 connects it to a real system.

This is Part 3 of my series on AI agents for SAP Plant Maintenance. In Part 1 I built the agent with CAP and Claude Desktop. In Part 2 I moved it to the governed MCP Gateway, but the data behind it was simulated by iFlows. This time there's an actual S/4HANA system on the other end.

What changed since Part 2: one box

Part 2 used simulated data. Part 3 adds a single new piece, the SAP Cloud Connector, and the agent reaches a real on-premise system.

The MCP side is almost the same as in Part 2. The MCP server runs on the Integration Cell of SAP Integration Suite and is generated from an API artifact, so I don't write or operate any server code. What's new is where the API points. It no longer points at a mock. It points at an on-premise S/4HANA, reached through the Cloud Connector.

If you haven't used the Cloud Connector before, think of it as a small agent installed on the SAP side of the network. It opens an outbound tunnel to SAP BTP, so nothing has to be opened inbound and the S/4HANA system is never exposed to the internet. SAP BTP can only reach the hosts and paths you explicitly allow, which in my case is one OData service.

How a question travels

Five hops, one outbound tunnel, real data back in a few seconds.

  1. You ask Claude Code something in plain language.
  2. The MCP server on SAP Integration Suite exposes the available tools, and Claude Code picks one.
  3. A governed API (OAuth, policies, monitoring) calls a BTP destination of type on-premise.
  4. The Cloud Connector carries the call through its tunnel into the network.
  5. SAP S/4HANA answers with the standard OData API for maintenance notifications (API_MAINTNOTIFICATION).

The round trip takes a few seconds. The agent only ever sees three read-only tools: list notifications, read one notification, and read its items.

Registering the server in Claude Code is a single command, because the same small stdio bridge from Part 2 handles the OAuth token:

claude mcp add sap-maintenance --scope user -- node bridge.js

From notifications to a dashboard

A chat answer is useful, but the real gain comes when the agent turns SAP data into something you can use. With the real notifications in context, it can write files, generate code and build pages from them.

I asked for a page with the open maintenance notifications of plant 1710, grouped by status and by equipment. The agent called the list tool, read the 13 open notifications from the test system, and built the dashboard:

The dashboard built from the 13 open notifications of plant 1710 in the test system.

13 open notifications: 5 with breakdown (M2) and 8 without (M1). All 13 are in status OSNO (outstanding), so the status view shows a single full bar. The agent kept NOPR, ORAS and NOCO on the chart with zero, to make it explicit that no notification is in those statuses instead of silently dropping them.

Clean core: what I changed in S/4HANA

  • Changed: activated one standard, SAP-released OData service (API_MAINTNOTIFICATION) in the Gateway.
  • Not changed: no ABAP, no custom objects, no inbound firewall ports, and no data replicated to SAP BTP (each call reads live from S/4HANA).

That matters beyond the demo. Agents reach SAP through a released API and a governed gateway, side by side with the core, which is the direction SAP recommends for third-party AI agents.

Three things that broke (so you don't lose the time I did)

  1. The API was created with no operations. Creating the API artifact from a destination left the OpenAPI spec empty. I pasted the spec in myself, with the three operations and their descriptions.
  2. Cloud Connector said "Not Reachable", but the server was up. The trace file showed the backend's TLS certificate had expired. On a test system, check certificates before you start debugging the network.
  3. My trial region wasn't in the Cloud Connector list. The trial runs on us10-001, and the right entry in the Cloud Connector is the main region host, cf.us10.

The agent stopped inventing

In Part 1 the agent got the data right but invented the meaning of a status code and built an answer on top of it. This time I put the meaning of the common statuses (open, in process, order assigned, completed) into the tool description, together with a plain rule: don't invent meanings for codes not on this list.

You can see it in the dashboard above: the status comes back from SAP as OSNO, and the agent reads it as outstanding because the tool description says so, not because it guessed.

MCP doesn't bring business context. The tool description does.

Honest limits

  • Test system, test data. It's a real S/4HANA 2023 on-premise QA system, but the notifications were created for this scenario. It's a feasibility demo, and it stays in testing.
  • About the video. It opens with a 5-second intro. After that, it shows the agent building the dashboard from the notifications in the test system.
  • Read-only, technical user. Every call reaches SAP with one technical identity. The next step for anything serious is principal propagation, so the SAP authorization of the person asking applies. This SAP post shows that path.
  • Trial tenant. Built on an SAP BTP trial. You can validate the pattern there before committing to a license.

If you're working on AI agents for SAP Plant Maintenance, EAM or asset management, let's talk in the comments or on LinkedIn.

Thanks for reading.

entry.title: Warehouse Process Type Determination for PMR in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud
entry.content:
Warehouse Process Type Determination for PMR in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud

Introduction

In SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition, warehouse process configuration plays an important role in ensuring the smooth movement of materials from the warehouse to Production Supply Areas (PSAs). In scenarios involving Scope Item 6NI – Production Supply with Kanban or Advanced Production Integration, the system uses Production Material Requests (PMRs) to support production supply processes.

While working with PMRs, you may notice an interesting behavior: the system automatically determines Warehouse Process Type (WPT) S220 for PMR items, even when no corresponding entry is visible in the standard Determine Warehouse Process Types configuration activity.

This raises a common question: How does SAP determine the warehouse process type when no visible configuration entry exists?

In this blog, we will explore this behavior, explain the role of SAP-delivered configuration, and clarify how the Assign Bin to PSA app influences warehouse task creation.

Details

  1. Understanding the scenario

In the Assign Bin to PSA app (App ID: /SCWM/PSASTAGE), users can maintain bin assignments for Production Supply Areas. These assignments support the staging of materials required for production.

For each material and PSA combination, you may expect the Warehouse Process Type to be determined based on the master data setup.

However, when you check the Determine Warehouse Process Types configuration activity, you may not find a visible entry specifically for PMR documents. Despite this, the system consistently determines WPT S220 for PMR items.

  1. The role of pre-delivered configuration

The behavior is associated with SAP-delivered configuration provided when Scope Item 6NI is activated.

According to this scenario, the system contains preconfigured entries for the following combination:

  • Document Type: PMRC
  • Item Type: PCC
  • Warehouse Process Type: S220

These entries are not visible in the standard configuration UI, but they support the standard PMR process.

As a result, the system automatically determines WPT S220 for PMR items without requiring users to manually maintain a corresponding entry in the configuration activity.

  1. How WPT determination works

The process can be understood in two parts:

Step 1: Default WPT determination

For PMR documents with document type PMRC and item type PCC, the system uses the pre-delivered configuration to determine WPT S220 by default.

Step 2: Staging warehouse task creation

During PSA staging task creation, the system also refers to the settings maintained in the Assign Bin to PSA app. These settings play a role in determining the picking warehouse process type used for the task.

If no applicable custom configuration changes the standard behavior, S220 is used as the default.

This approach supports consistent warehouse process determination while reducing the need for additional manual configuration in standard production supply scenarios.

  1. What should you consider during implementation?

When configuring production supply in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud, keep the following points in mind:

  • Understand the standard behavior: S220 is the default WPT for the PMRC/PCC combination in the described scenario.
  • Review PSA bin assignments: Check the Assign Bin to PSA app when validating picking task creation and warehouse process type behavior.
  • Avoid unnecessary configuration: Additional entries may not be required if the standard SAP-delivered behavior meets the business requirement.
  • Validate custom requirements: If the business process requires a different WPT, investigate the available configuration options and their effect on task creation before making changes.

Understanding this behavior can save troubleshooting time when the system determines a WPT even though no corresponding entry is visible in the configuration UI.

Conclusion

When a warehouse process type is determined automatically in SAP S/4HANA Public Cloud, the absence of a visible configuration entry does not necessarily mean that the system lacks the configuration needed to support the process.

Warehouse Process Type determination for PMRs in SAP S/4HANA Cloud, Public Edition, Scope Item 6NI, demonstrates how SAP-delivered configuration supports standard production supply processes.

The key takeaways are:

  • SAP provides pre-delivered configuration for the PMRC document type and PCC item type combination.
  • WPT S220 is the default in the scenario described.
  • The corresponding configuration entries may not be visible in the standard Determine Warehouse Process Types activity.
  • The Assign Bin to PSA app remains relevant when determining the picking WPT during warehouse task creation.
  • Manual configuration should be considered only when the standard behavior does not meet the required business process.

By understanding the relationship between PMR document types, item types, default WPT determination, and PSA bin assignments, SAP EWM consultants can troubleshoot production supply scenarios more effectively and avoid unnecessary configuration changes.

entry.title: Introducing Joule Studio Certification: Build real-world AI Skills. Practice. Prove What You Can Do.
entry.content:
We are proud to announce a brand new SAP Certification for developers and solution architects, building AI agents, applications, and workflows with Joule Studio, with one certification attempt available at no cost from September 30 through December 31, 2026.

AI is changing how software is built. And as development changes, so do the skills developers need to turn new ideas into solutions that work in the enterprise context.

For SAP developers and technical professionals, that increasingly means knowing how to move beyond understanding AI concepts to actually building with AI: creating agents, applications, and workflows, grounding them in business context, and managing them from development through deployment, and at scale.

SAP Certification is evolving alongside those skills.

This year marks 30 years of SAP Certification. Over three decades, certification has evolved alongside SAP technology, from the SAP R/3 era to today's cloud and AI-enabled enterprise landscape. Over the past year, that evolution has accelerated as SAP has reimagined certification around practical skills and how professionals actually work.

Now, we’re taking another leap forward with a new certification focused on agentic development.

From knowledge to practical skills

Over the past year, SAP has been reimagining its certification approach, shifting from traditional knowledge-based testing toward practical, performance-based assessments that reflect how professionals work. Rather than focusing on what learners can recall, the emphasis is now on demonstrating how they apply their skills to realistic challenges. The new Joule Studio Certification builds on this approach, validating the practical capabilities needed to develop AI agents, applications, and workflows.

Introducing Joule Studio Certification

Available now, the Joule Studio Developer Certification is a new SAP Certification for developers and technical professionals building and extending AI agents, applications, and workflows with Joule Studio, SAP’s AI-first development environment on the SAP Business AI Platform.

The certification provides a structured way to demonstrate practical proficiency with Joule Studio, from translating an idea into an agent to grounding that agent in SAP business context and managing its deployment and lifecycle.

It is designed for developers and technical professionals across the SAP ecosystem who want to demonstrate their ability to put AI development skills into practice.

What will the certification cover?

The Joule Studio Certification focuses on skills involved in taking AI development from idea to implementation.

These include:

  • Intent-based development: Translating a business idea into a deployable agent using Joule Studio’s natural-language-driven development experience.
  • Building and extending AI agents: Creating custom agents or extending LoB agents to address specific business needs.
  • Business context: Grounding agents in relevant SAP business data, processes, and context.
  • Deployment and lifecycle management: Managing, testing, and deploying agents and skills throughout their lifecycle.

Together, these capabilities reflect the broader value of Joule Studio: enabling developers to build AI agents, applications, and workflows grounded in business context, using development tools that fit their needs, with governance and security built in.

Most importantly, the certification is about demonstrating that these capabilities can be applied in practice.

Why practical validation matters for AI

AI development is moving quickly. New tools and capabilities continue to emerge, but knowing that a technology exists is very different from knowing how to use it effectively.

For developers, the real value comes from being able to take a business need and turn it into something useful: identifying the right approach, grounding AI in the appropriate context, building and extending capabilities, and managing what has been created.

That is why practical skills validation is an important part of SAP’s evolving certification approach.

As SAP advances its AI-first development strategy, certification can provide professionals with a way to demonstrate that they are not simply familiar with emerging technologies but can apply them to real development scenarios.

entry.title: Re: How to Manually Distribute Available Stock Among Mult...
entry.content:
Dear @SumitSagar,

Yes, manual redistribution of confirmed quantities between Sales Orders is supported using Release for Delivery (F1786) part of Advanced ATP (scope item 1JW)

I configured the required responsibility in Configure Order Fulfillment Responsibilities (F2246) and tested two Sales Orders for the same material and plant but different Sold-to Parties

Test results:

  • SO 1407: Ordered 15 PC, confirmed quantity reduced from 5 to 3 PC

  • SO 2829: Ordered 10 PC, confirmed quantity increased from 0 to 7 PC (2 PC redistributed from SO 1407 and 5 PC from previously available ATP quantity)

After selecting Publish and Back I verified both Sales Orders in Display Sales Orders (VA03). The Schedule Lines confirmed the new quantities of 3 PC and 7 PC while the original ordered quantities remained unchanged

Recommended procedure:

  1. Configure the relevant responsibility and assign the user in F2246

  2. Open Release for Delivery (F1786) and select the material and plant

  3. Manually adjust the confirmed quantities for the relevant Sales Order items

  4. Select Publish and Back and verify the updated Schedule Lines

The same approach can be used for your proposed distribution of 25, 30 and 45 PC, provided sufficient ATP quantity is available and the Sales Order items are eligible for processing

Please note that Release for Delivery requires Advanced ATP (1JW), which requires an additional license. Certain Sales Order items may also be restricted from manual changes as described in SAP KBA 3581003

If Backorder Processing (BOP) is configured to process these Sales Orders, subsequent BOP runs may change the manually assigned confirmations depending on the confirmation strategy. I recommend reviewing the relevant BOP variants. I did not test this behavior

Since I successfully tested manual redistribution using standard functionality no custom development or API-based solution is required for this scenario

More details below:

SAP Help – Solve Issues by Redistributing Quantities

SAP Help – How to Configure Order Fulfillment Responsibilities

SAP KBA 3581003 – FAQ: Release for Delivery (R4D) – Public Cloud Edition

Best Regards,

Dawid

entry.title: ABAP Debugger Enhancement — Reloaded: Typed VALUE Statements and What's Changed Since 2019
entry.content:
This post was first published on LinkedIn. A German version is available on the T5 website.

The debugger often shows you exactly the data you need for a unit test — and then you end up retyping it by hand. DDVE (Debugger Data View Extension) saves you that step: one click, and you get a ready-to-paste VALUE statement. The latest update makes that statement typed and closes a few long-standing gaps — and since the last blog post in 2019, the community has contributed quite a bit as well.

How it works

DDVE adds a “Data for ABAP View” entry to the debugger in three places: the Services of the Tool menus of the table and structure tools, and the toolbar of the table's ALV display. The result is a syntactically correct, pretty-printed statement like this, ready to be copied into your test method:

" One click in the debugger turns the content of LT_FLIGHTS into:
DATA(lt_flights) = VALUE tt_flights(
  ( carrid = 'LH' connid = '0400' fldate = '20260115' price = '666.00' currency = 'EUR' )
  ( carrid = 'LH' connid = '0402' fldate = '20260116' price = '471.00' currency = 'EUR' )
  ( carrid = 'AA' connid = '0017' fldate = '20260117' price = '422.94' currency = 'USD' ) ).

 

The custom entry “Data for ABAP View” in the service menu of the table or structure view

The result popup with the generated, ready-to-paste VALUE statement

Under the hood, DDVE plugs into the standard debugger through three implicit enhancements — no modifications. All three hand over to the same pipeline: read the real data, resolve the type, render the VALUE statement, then format and show it.

Architecture overview: three implicit enhancements in the standard ABAP debugger hand over to the DDVE pipeline

 

New name, new home

If you know the tool from my earlier posts here on SAP Community from 2017 and 2019: it has since been refactored, extended and renamed, and it now lives in a new GitHub repository:

https://github.com/gepparta/abap_debugger_data_view_extension

I was also happy to find DDVE in the DSAG ABAP guide: the ABAP guidelines of the German-speaking SAP user group list it as the SAP GUI option for generating VALUE statements from debugger data.

All classes follow the ZCL_DDVE_* naming scheme. New in this update:

  1. Typed VALUE statements with inline declarations — DATA(flights) = VALUE flighttab( ... ) instead of an untyped #
  2. Robustness fixes for nested data in filtered exports, anonymous runtime types and empty tables and structures
  3. A refactored core with a much broader unit test suite

And since 2019, the community has contributed an ALV export that respects filters, hidden columns and sort order, .INCLUDE support and fixes for hashed tables — more on that below.

 

New in this update

1. Typed VALUE statements with inline declaration

Until now the generated statement looked like lt_flights = VALUE #( ... ) — fine as long as the target variable already exists and the compiler can infer the type. In a fresh unit test it usually can't.

Typed statements were an old feature request by Timo John — now they're here. DDVE resolves the variable's type from the debugger context and generates a self-contained inline declaration:

" DDIC type
DATA(table_of_flights) = VALUE flighttab( ( carrid = 'AA' connid = '0017' ) ).

" type declared inside a global class
DATA(item) = VALUE zcl_order=>ty_item( col1 = 1 ).

The interesting part is what counts as a usable type name. The debugger reports absolute type names such as \CLASS=ZCL_ORDER\TYPE=TY_ITEM or \PROGRAM=ZREP\TYPE=TY_LOCAL. Where no usable type or variable name can be derived — e.g. for a component path like LS_X-COMP — DDVE gracefully falls back to the classic untyped VALUE #( ... ), since DATA(...) with # would not compile. A new class ZCL_DDVE_TYPE_RESOLVER translates the debugger's type names into source-code-valid expressions:

Debugger type name Generated expression Why it works in a test

\TYPE=SFLIGHTsflightDDIC, visible everywhere
\CLASS=ZCL_X\TYPE=TY_Yzcl_x=>ty_ypublic always, private via LOCAL FRIENDS
\INTERFACE=ZIF_X\TYPE=TY_Yzif_x=>ty_yinterface components are public
\PROGRAM=ZREP\TYPE=TY_LOCALty_localtest include sits in the same program
\TYPE-POOL=ABAP\TYPE=ABAP_BOOLabap_booltype pools are global
procedure-local / generated typesfallback #not addressable from a test

2. Robustness fixes for the tricky cases

A couple of long-standing edge cases are gone:

  • Nested data in filtered exports — since the filter support from 2023 (see the community section below), nested tables and structures in the ALV export came out as placeholder texts like COL2 = `Structure: flat, not charlike` . When the debugger's ALV works on an internal copy of the table, DDVE now re-reads the real data and uses the ALV view only as a row and column mask — filters, hidden columns and sort order still apply, and nested data keeps its real values.
  • Anonymous runtime types — inline declared table types, OCCURS header lines, TYPE HANDLE structures — are now reconstructed from debugger metadata instead of silently producing no output popup at all.
  • Empty tables and structures produce a valid empty VALUE statement instead of broken output.

3. A refactored core with a broader test suite

The 2019 post already talked about single responsibility; this iteration went further. Rendering of VALUE expressions now lives in a dedicated class (ZCL_DDVE_VALUE_RENDERER) that owns the entire recursion for nested data, while the debugger facades for tables and structures only orchestrate. Output (CL_DEMO_OUTPUT), customizing access and pretty-printer creation are isolated behind their own small classes — which is precisely why the package now comes with a much broader ABAP Unit test suite, most of it mock-free.

Since 2019: contributions from the community

Between 2020 and 2023, several pull requests made it into the tool without ever getting a blog post of their own. If you still run the 2019 version, they are new for you as well.

What you see is what you get

Thanks to Daniel Wegner (@WegnerDan), the export respects what you see in the debugger's ALV:

  • Rows filtered out in the ALV are excluded from the generated statement.
  • Columns hidden in the ALV layout (no_out) are skipped.
  • The export follows the current ALV sort order.
  • The ALV's technical INDEX column no longer ends up in the generated statement.

So you can shape your test data visually in the ALV before exporting it — a surprisingly effective way to cut a 500-row production table down to the three rows that actually reproduce your bug.

More contributions

  • .INCLUDE structures — @juancarlosrodriguezf made sure that structures containing .INCLUDEs (e.g. a local type that includes T000 plus extra fields) are flattened correctly into the field catalog. Previously the included components were lost; the fix ships with its own unit test.
  • Hashed tables and performance — @sandraros contributed faster statement generation plus fixes for hashed tables and for tables with a component named INDEX.
  • Pretty printer and housekeeping — Andreas Kopp (@andkopp) fixed details in the pretty printer, and Christian Günter (@christianguenter2) brought the repository in line with the current abapGit format and fixed a syntax error.

Thanks to everyone who contributed! Two related posts here on SAP Community: Fork of ABAP Debugger Data View Extension tool and Speed up regression tests with the ABAP debugger, which uses the tool to create test data for regression tests.

A note on the built-in pretty printer

The 2019 post made quite a fuss about pretty printing the generated VALUE statement — including the option to plug in your own printer implementation via a pretty printer interface (today ZIF_DDVE_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER) and the customizing table ZTOP_DVE_CUST.

Honestly, this part has become less important: with ABAP Cleaner there is now an excellent open source formatter that aligns VALUE constructor expressions beautifully in ADT. So a perfectly fine workflow today is: export the raw statement with DDVE, paste it into your test method, and let ABAP Cleaner take care of the formatting.

The built-in pretty printers (and the customizing mechanism) are still there and still useful if you want a readable preview right in the SAP GUI popup — but if you are an ADT + ABAP Cleaner user, don't worry too much about this feature.

Migrating from the old installation

If you still run the original version (ZCL_OP_* classes), note that the enhancement implementations and the customizing table have the same names in both versions. Therefore:

  1. Export your ZTOP_DVE_CUST entries (if any).
  2. Uninstall the old package via abapGit (Uninstall/Purge).
  3. Pull the DDVE repository.
  4. Re-import your customizing and map the class names: ZCL_OP_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER → ZCL_DDVE_VALUE_PRETTY_PRINTER, ZCL_MAX_LINE_LENGTH_PP → ZCL_DDVE_MAX_LINE_LENGTH_PP.

Do not install both versions in parallel.

Prerequisites

NetWeaver ABAP 7.40 SP08 or higher.

How to install

All the coding is available here:

https://github.com/gepparta/abap_debugger_data_view_extension

Please use abapGit to get the coding into your system.

Pull requests and issues on GitHub are welcome.

Hands up: who has already used the extension? Or have you all moved on to ADT or VS Code and left the SAP GUI debugger behind – or is AI writing your unit tests by now anyway? Let me know in the comments.

entry.title: What's New in SAP Automation Pilot – Q3 2026
entry.content:
SAP Automation Pilot ships 15 new features in Q3 2026 – including native AI-agent authentication, a persistent key-value storage shared across executions, and over 60 new provided commands.

If you're running automations on SAP Business Technology Platform (BTP), your toolkit just got a serious upgrade. This quarter touches everything from how you connect to external systems, to how automations persist data between runs, to how you track what's actually happening across your landscape. Here's the full picture.

 

New to the product?​

It's a low-code/no-code automation service on SAP BTP that helps DevOps and Operations teams automate cloud operations – with over 300 built-in commands and a serverless script execution environment. More details about the product can be found at:

  • SAP Automation Pilot Documentation

Usage Statistics Dashboard

SAP Automation Pilot now has a built-in dashboard that shows you how your automations are actually being used. You can see the number of executions by day and hour, which commands get triggered most, success rates, and how much of your quota you've consumed – all with time-range filtering. If you've been piecing this picture together manually or through external tools, it's now right inside the service. For more information, see Working with Executions.

Subexecutions Panel in Execution Details

When you open an execution's details page, there's now a dedicated Subexecutions section that lists everything the parent execution triggered. Subexecutions also get tagged automatically – autopi:parentExecutorPath tells you which executor started them, and for ParallelForEach, autopi:parentBatchIndex tells you which batch they belonged to. No more jumping back and forth to understand what a complex command actually did. For more information, see Monitoring Executions.

Capture HTTP User-Agent as a Service Tag

When an external system triggers an execution via the API, SAP Automation Pilot now reads the User-Agent header from the HTTP request and stores it as a read-only autopi:userAgent service tag. This means that even when multiple systems share the same service account, you can tell which one triggered which execution – directly from the details page or by filtering via the API. It takes zero configuration on the SAP Automation Pilot side – the caller just needs to set a meaningful User-Agent header, which is a one-line change in any HTTP request. For more information, see Tags.

Configurable Table Columns with Custom Tag-Based Columns

The entity tables in SAP Automation Pilot – Commands, Inputs, Executions, Scheduled Executions – can now be personalized. You can show or hide predefined columns, reorder them, and add custom columns based on your tag keys. So if your team tags executions by environment, region, or ticket number, those values can now show up as their own columns instead of being buried inside each execution's detail view. For more information, see Configuring Table Columns.

Command Clone with Multiple Cloning Modes

Cloning commands now gives you three distinct modes. Clone Full Command copies the entire configuration into a new command, so you can adapt and extend it without touching the source – this one is available for custom commands. Clone Contract Only keeps the same input and output keys but gives you an empty implementation to build from scratch. Clone as Wrapper creates a new command with a single executor that calls the source command, with all parameters automatically mapped – so you can add logic around it without reconfiguring anything manually. Both Clone Contract Only and Clone as Wrapper are available for provided commands as well, giving you a proper starting point when building on top of SAP-provided content. For more information, see Cloning Commands.

Secure Service Account Integration for AI Agents

Service accounts in SAP Automation Pilot now support token-based authentication – meaning the credentials can be used as a Bearer token or an API key, on top of the existing Basic authentication. The service account type has been renamed to API Token / Basic and the password field is now called token to reflect this.

 

 

Why does this matter? Because MCP clients, Joule, and most third-party agent frameworks expect token-based auth. Until now, wiring them into SAP Automation Pilot required workarounds. Now it's a native, one-step setup. Alongside this, a new MCP permission lets you scope exactly which MCP server endpoints a service account can access – so you can give an AI agent the ability to trigger automations without granting access to anything beyond what the agent needs.

If you're building agent-driven Ops workflows, this is the feature that makes it practical. For more information, see Managing Service Account Permissions.

Native Destination Service Integration & HTTP Request Enhancements

The new HttpRequestViaDestination command lets you execute HTTP requests by referencing a destination from the SAP Destination Service directly. URL resolution, authentication, proxy settings, certificates – all of it is pulled from the destination configuration automatically. No more duplicating credentials and connection details inside SAP Automation Pilot. If you're already managing your connectivity through the SAP Destination Service, your automations can now plug straight into that setup. For more information see HTTP Operations (http-sapcp) Catalog.

SendEmail STARTTLS Support

The SendEmail command now supports STARTTLS encryption through a new encryptionMode input key. Previously, sending emails through public SMTP servers that require STARTTLS meant routing traffic through SAP Cloud Connector. Now you can connect directly – one less hop, one less thing to configure. For more information, see Email Operations (email-sapcp) Catalog.

Cross-Execution Runtime Storage

Until now, each execution in SAP Automation Pilot lived in isolation – once it finished, its data went with it. That changes with the new Cross-Execution Runtime Storage: a tenant-scoped, encrypted key/value storage that any execution can read from and write to. Three commands handle everything – PutValue, GetValue, and DeleteValue.

This unlocks automation scenarios that simply weren't practical before. Executions can now pass state to each other, track progress across multi-step workflows, cache shared configuration, or coordinate processes – all without relying on external storage. If you've ever built a workaround to share data between executions, this is the clean, built-in replacement. For more information, see Execution Runtime Storage.

SAP Integration Suite Provided Catalog

SAP Automation Pilot now ships a dedicated catalog for SAP Integration Suite – 21 ready-to-use commands covering integration flow lifecycle management, configuration updates, monitoring of deployed integration flows, and directory management. All accessible directly from the provided catalogs, no custom command building required.

This is a significant expansion. SAP Integration Suite is one of the most widely used services on SAP BTP, and until now, automating operations around it meant building everything from scratch using HTTP requests. With a provided catalog in place, teams can automate routine integration operations – deploying flows, checking statuses, updating configurations.

If you're managing integration landscapes at scale, this catalog saves a lot of custom work. For more information, see SAP Integration Suite (is-sapcp) Catalog.

SAP HANA Cloud Lifecycle Management Commands

A new SAP HANA Cloud Administration catalog brings 40 commands for managing SAP HANA Cloud instances – covering provisioning, lifecycle management, configuration, and observability across both Cloud Foundry and Other Environment deployment types.
We covered this catalog in depth in a dedicated blog post – you can find it here: Meet the SAP HANA Cloud Administration Catalog for SAP Automation Pilot

Granular Skip Options for ParallelForEach Failures

When a ParallelForEach step fails, the Skip dialog now offers two distinct options – skip only the current failed batch and continue processing the remaining ones, or skip all remaining batches and move on to the next executor in the parent command. Previously, skipping meant stopping everything. Now you can isolate a failure without halting the entire parallel run. For more information, see Controlling Executions with Actions.

Custom Tags for ParallelForEach Subexecutions

You can now assign tags to ParallelForEach subexecutions dynamically using expressions. Instead of entering tags manually for each subexecution, you reference a complete tag set from an input and it gets applied automatically, making it easier to organize, filter, and trace parallel workloads at scale. For more information, see ParallelForEach.

Auto-Abort Stale Failed Executions

A new Auto-Abort Failed Executions feature automatically aborts executions that remain in a Failed state without updates for a configurable duration (1–168 hours). Your execution list stays clean without manual intervention. For more information, see Additional Features.

Immediate Deletion of Completed Executions

You can now delete completed executions on the spot instead of waiting for the retention cleanup cycle. Setting the retention value to 0 causes immediate deletion as soon as an execution reaches a completed status. When an execution is done and you no longer need it, it's gone, keeping your execution list manageable without relying on automated retention policies. For more information, see Additional Features.

Learn More & Stay Connected

  • SAP Road Map Explorer for SAP Automation Pilot

  • Release Navigator for SAP Automation Pilot - find release notes, blog posts, and related resources in one place

The Generate Compliance Forms option is displayed based on the following conditions:

  1. The candidate’s job country, job location, or home address country is either Canada or the United States.

  2. The required country and state compliance configurations are correctly configured and functional for the Onboarding module under Compliance Settings.

  3. Under Compliance Settings, the Compliance Forms Accessibility in Other Modules switch is enabled for either the United States or Canada, as applicable.

If any of these conditions are not met, the Generate Compliance Forms option will not be displayed. Please note that this option is currently not permission-controlled.

If you do not want employees to access these forms, you can disable the Compliance Forms Accessibility in Other Modules switch under Compliance Settings for the relevant country (This option is disabled by default).

Note: If a candidate was initiated through Onboarding and has already been assigned a country compliance form, clicking Generate Compliance Forms will trigger a validation to check whether a compliance process is already associated with the candidate. The system will initiate a new compliance process only if one does not already exist.

entry.title: New Pattern: Migrating Content-Based Routing Synchronous Scenarios to SAP IS using Migration Tool
entry.content:
This blog post is part of the series Master Blog: SAP Process Orchestration to SAP Integration Suite Migration – Tool and Guidance . In this edition, we focus specifically on migrating Content-Based Routing (CBR) Synchronous Scenarios to SAP Integration Suite using the Migration Tool.  

What This Blog Covers

The Migration Tool in SAP Integration Suite now supports CBR Synchronous scenarios. This post walks you through everything you need to migrate one: 

  • What makes a CBR scenario synchronous  and the one constraint that sets it apart from async CBR 
  • The eight supported CBR Standard Synchronous cases, broken down by operations, receivers, and interfaces 
  • How the Migration Tool detects the pattern from your ICO automatically 
  • What the Standard Approach generates, and where it differs from the async migration 
  • How the Pipeline Approach works : the three flows, the Partner Directory, and the receiverDetermination XSLT 
  • What to check before you go live

Understanding Synchronous Content-Based Routing in SAP PO 

In a Content-Based Routing scenario, a message does not arrive with a fixed destination. The runtime inspects the message payload, evaluates it against the conditions defined in Receiver Determination, and selects the receiver at that moment. The routing is governed entirely by the content of the message: a field value, an element, or a structure within the payload. 

In practice, this means the following: 

  • Several receivers are configured, and each is associated with its own routing condition. 
  • The decision is dynamic. The same configuration can deliver different messages to different systems according to their content. 
  • A receiver may require the message in a specific format. Through Interface Determination, the same incoming message can be mapped differently depending on which receiver is selected. 

If you are new to Content-Based Routing (CBR) in SAP PO, we recommend first reading our earlier blog Migrating Content-Based Routing Scenarios Using th... - SAP Community  which explains how CBR works, including Receiver Determination and Interface Determination in detail. 

On top of everything CBR already does, the synchronous variant adds one thing: the sender waits for a response.

What Makes it Synchronous? 

Three things together define this as a synchronous scenario: 

  • Both sides use synchronous interfaces

             In SAP PO, a synchronous service interface defines both a request message and a corresponding response message. It's a two-way contract from the start something goes in, something comes back. An asynchronous interface only defines one direction. 

  • Two-Directional Message Mappings

             Because the sender and receiver typically have different formats, two mappings are required:

  •     Request Mapping : transforms the sender's payload into the format the receiver expects 
  •     Response Mapping : transforms the receiver's reply into the format the sender expects 
  • The Connection Stays Open 

             The sender sends the message and waits. It doesn't move on until a reply comes back on the same connection. If something  goes wrong such as a routing issue, a mapping failure, a timeout the sender still needs an answer. Even if it's an error, the caller is waiting. 

            One rule that changes everything 

             In asynchronous CBR, you can route to multiple receivers at once, each gets their own copy. Synchronous doesn't work that way. The sender is waiting for one response, so the routing must land on exactly one receiver and one interface. This means your routing conditions need to be set up so only one can ever match at a time. If two conditions match the same message, things break. If none match, the scenario must throw an error because the sender hasn't moved on yet and is still waiting for a reply. 

Migration of CBR synchronous scenarios using Standard approach and Pipeline approach 

Supported Scenarios in CBR Standard Synchronous 

Every one of these uses a Local Rule with XPath for the routing conditions. 

One thing to keep in mind: when you have N receivers, each one needs its own routing condition, otherwise the scenario isn't valid.
